This was verified first-hand against published tarballs by two independent passes.

---

### 16.1 Assistive Access: the separate, simplified Photos app

Assistive Access (iOS 17+) is a cognitively-simplified device mode set up by a trusted supporter. It does **not** run the normal Photos app in a smaller frame — it substitutes a distinct, flat Photos experience.

**What Apple's AA Photos actually is.** A person using Assistive Access "can use the Photos app to view photos, videos, and selfies captured in the Camera app, as well as pictures and videos from shared albums." The IA is deliberately flat: one photo surface; tap a photo to view it; and "[o]n any screen in Assistive Access, the person using Assistive Access can always tap Back to return to the previous screen." There is no Library/Memories/Albums/Search/People tab structure, no editing surface, and no sharing surface documented. (Note: the absence of those tabs is an argument from absence — no Apple doc contradicts it, but none enumerates the exclusions either.)

**Setup path:** Settings > Accessibility > Assistive Access > Manage Apps > add Photos.

**Exactly two toggles exist. There is no third.**

| Toggle | Apple's exact behavior |
|---|---|
| **Include Shared Albums** | "To show pictures and videos in the Photos app from albums that are shared with the person using Assistive Access, turn on Include Shared Albums, then select the Shared Albums to include, or create one." If off: "the Photos app shows only the photos and videos that the person using Assistive Access captures in the Camera app." |
| **Pinch to Zoom** | "To allow the person using Assistive Access to zoom in on their photos, turn on Pinch to Zoom." |

Content scoping is done at the **source** level, not by filtering. Default scope = only Camera-captured items on this device; optional scope = plus supporter-selected Shared Albums. Zoom is a **capability gate**, not a view state.

**System-wide layout** is chosen at Settings > Accessibility > Assistive Access > Rows or Grid: "a row layout that makes it easier to read items in a list, or a large grid that emphasizes images and icons."

**Apps Apple designed for Assistive Access** (per the AA user guide table of contents): Calls, Camera, Messages, Music, Photos, Magnifier, Apple TV.

#### 16.1.1 Behavioral divergences in AA that break normal app assumptions

Apple documents explicit divergences. The one that is a crash-class bug for a photo app:

> "To minimize pop-ups while using iPhone, apps won't ask for permission to access information such as location, photos, and contacts. Instead, you have the option to set access permissions for apps when you set up Assistive Access. To review or change an app's permissions, you must exit Assistive Access and go to Settings > Accessibility > Assistive Access or Settings > Apps > [app name]."

Permissions are pre-granted (or denied) by the trusted supporter at setup time. **Your app's runtime permission request will not present a prompt.**

Other documented divergences:
- No Settings app and no notifications inside AA ("there is no Settings app or notifications in Assistive Access").
- Software updates require exiting AA.
- Status icons are not shown: network, Focus, Bluetooth, Location Services indicator, **and Airplane Mode**.
- "Emergency SOS via satellite isn't available in Assistive Access."
- **Crash Detection CONTINUES to work in Assistive Access** — "If Crash Detection is available and enabled on the iPhone, it will continue to work in Assistive Access." This is the **opposite** of Guided Access, where Crash Detection and Emergency Services are explicitly disabled (§16.6). Do not treat the two lockdown modes as equivalently restrictive.

⚠️ **Trap:** An app that hard-blocks its first-run flow on a permission prompt is simply *broken* inside Assistive Access. The user sees a dead screen, the prompt never appears, and there is no Settings app to escape to. Our first run requests **both** Photo Library access (PHPhotoLibrary) **and** Local Network permission (for LAN pairing to the desktop node). Neither prompt will render in AA.

#### 16.1.2 The third-party Assistive Access API (iOS/iPadOS 26)

iOS/iPadOS 26 opened Assistive Access to third-party apps. This is the biggest single opportunity in this domain.

| Mechanism | What it does |
|---|---|
| `UISupportsAssistiveAccess` (Info.plist, YES) | Apple: "Adding the UISupportsAssistiveAccess key to your project's Info pane with a value of YES indicates your app supports a streamlined experience designed for Assistive Access… It also lists your app as Optimized for Assistive Access in Settings." |
| SwiftUI `AssistiveAccess` scene | New scene type, introduced iOS 26.0 / iPadOS 26.0. The streamlined UI you present in AA. |
| `UISupportsFullScreenInAssistiveAccess` (Info.plist, YES) | "allows your app's standard UI to expand into all the available space above the Back button." |
| `AccessibilitySettings.isAssistiveAccessEnabled` (Accessibility framework) | Runtime detection. |
| SwiftUI `EnvironmentValues.accessibilityAssistiveAccessEnabled` | Runtime detection in SwiftUI. |

Non-optimized apps still run, but degraded: "the system draws apps in a reduced frame to fit them onscreen with the prominent Back button… This frame matches the dimensions of a smaller iPhone or iPad screen." Apple's guidance for the AA scene is to "remove workflows or UI elements that aren't appropriate in the context of Assistive Access."

⚠️ **Trap for React Native:** The `AssistiveAccess` scene is **SwiftUI-only**. An RN app gets `UISupportsFullScreenInAssistiveAccess` for free (it is just an Info.plist key, settable from Expo app config), but a real streamlined AA experience **cannot be built in JavaScript**. It requires a native Swift scene mounted alongside the RN root. Budget a native iOS module; do not assume RN covers it.

**Android has no Assistive Access equivalent.** Whether any Android OEM ships a comparable simplified mode is an **open research item** — not investigated by the corpus.

---

### 16.2 VoiceOver Recognition — the OS describing photos we failed to label

Settings > Accessibility > VoiceOver > **VoiceOver Recognition** has **three** toggles: Image Descriptions, Text Recognition, and **Screen Recognition**. All three are on-device fallbacks that fire *only when the app provides no label*. Device floor for all: iPhone XS / XS Max / XR or later, iOS 14+.

#### 16.2.1 Image Descriptions

> "When Image Descriptions is on, VoiceOver describes images in apps and on the web. When using the Camera app to take a photo, VoiceOver also describes what's visible in the viewfinder. VoiceOver lets you know if an image has sensitive content before it describes the image."

**Feedback Style** controls the announcement prefix:

| Style | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **Speak** | "VoiceOver first says 'possibly,' then it describes what it recognizes." |
| **Play Sound** | Apple's illustrative output here: "A black dog lying on a blue and white blanket on a wooden floor." (⚠️ **Trap:** this example belongs to the **Play Sound** style specifically — it is *not* a generic Image Descriptions output sample. Do not cite it as one.) |
| **Do Nothing** | No prefix. |

To repeat a description: **"use three fingers to tap on an image."**

**Supported languages — two Apple sources disagree, and the discrepancy is real (independently reproduced by the fact-checker).**

| Source | Count | Languages |
|---|---|---|
| `apple.com/ios/feature-availability` (current, iOS 26) — **treat as authoritative** | **12** | Arabic; English (United Kingdom); English (United States); French (France); German (Germany); Italian (Italy); **Japanese**; Korean; Mandarin Chinese (China mainland); Portuguese (Brazil); Russian; Spanish (Spain) |
| Support article **111799** (Published May 21, 2024; note: no "HT" prefix on the current URL) | **11** | Same set **minus Japanese** |

No changelog explaining when Japanese was added was found.

**No public API.** There is no way to invoke Image Descriptions programmatically and no way to read the generated string. It is a VoiceOver-layer fallback, not a developer service. The only lever we have is the inverse: **if we set `accessibilityLabel`, VoiceOver reads ours and Image Descriptions does not fire.**

#### 16.2.2 Text Recognition (OCR inside photos)

> "When Text Recognition is on, VoiceOver reads the text it identifies within images and photos. Text Recognition is available in Chinese (Simplified), Chinese (Traditional), English (U.S.), French (France), German (Germany), Italian (Italy), Portuguese (Brazil), and Spanish (Spain)."

**8 languages** — notably missing Japanese, Korean, Arabic, and Russian, all of which Image Descriptions *does* support.

Apple also documents structured reading order: it lets you "navigate nutrition labels and receipts in the order items are listed." (This phrasing lives on the iPhone User Guide live-descriptions page, not in article 111799.)

Not directly hookable — but the *capability* is available to us: Apple's Vision framework `VNRecognizeTextRequest` does on-device OCR, and our desktop compute node can OCR at ingest and surface the recognized text as accessible content.

#### 16.2.3 Screen Recognition

> "When Screen Recognition is on, VoiceOver recognizes an app's interface controls to help you navigate it."

Sits alongside Image Descriptions and Text Recognition in the same settings pane. **This is the fallback users lean on when an app's controls are unlabeled** — i.e. it is precisely the mechanism that makes a custom RN photo grid with unlabeled overlay buttons "sort of work" while looking broken.

#### 16.2.4 Explore Image — finger-drag spatial exploration

Apple's exact flow:

> "Go to an app such as Photos or Safari, then select an image. Swipe up to hear more options, then double-tap when you hear Explore Image. Move your finger around the image to find out the position of each object."

Purpose: "You can move your finger over a photo to discover a person's position relative to other objects." Requires Image Descriptions on; Text Recognition adds in-image text.

Mechanically, **Explore Image is a VoiceOver *action*** (surfaced via the actions rotor / swipe-up on the focused image). Activating it switches VoiceOver into a direct-touch spatial mode over the image.

**It is replicable.** The mechanism is UIKit accessibility custom actions plus per-region child accessibility elements with `accessibilityFrame` / `accessibilityFrameInContainerSpace`, so VoiceOver's direct-touch exploration hits them.

⚠️ **Trap:** This is **not expressible in React Native's standard props.** `accessibilityActions` / `onAccessibilityAction` gives you the *action*, but per-region hit-testable sub-elements *inside a single image* require a native view: a UIView subclass overriding `accessibilityElementCount` / `accessibilityElement(at:)` on iOS, and a custom `ExploreByTouchHelper` / `AccessibilityNodeProvider` virtual view hierarchy on Android. Do not attempt this in JS.

#### 16.2.5 Live Recognition / Point & Speak — adjacent, and it reserves gestures

Not a Photos feature (it is a camera/world feature), but it **claims multi-finger gestures system-wide when VoiceOver is on**, which constrains our gesture design.

- **"With VoiceOver on, triple-tap the screen with four fingers to start Live Recognition."**
- Categories the user toggles: **Scenes, People, Doors, Furniture, Text, and Point & Speak**.
- "If you turn on Point & Speak, you can point your finger at text and have VoiceOver read it aloud."
- "To interrupt VoiceOver speech and move to the next detected item, tap the screen with two fingers."
- Exit: another four-finger triple-tap, or a two-finger scrub — "move two fingers back and forth three times quickly, making a 'z'".
- Settings: "To change Live Recognition settings, go to the Magnifier app, tap, then tap Detect."
- Availability caveat, in Apple's exact words: "Detection of people, doors, and furniture is available only on supported iPhone models." (The corpus's original gloss "LiDAR-class" was a researcher **inference**, not Apple's words — do not repeat it as sourced.)
- Apple's safety caveat, verbatim: "VoiceOver Recognition should not be relied upon in circumstances where you could be harmed or injured, in high-risk situations, for navigation, or for the diagnosis or treatment of any medical condition."

**Gestures the system claims when VoiceOver is on** (so we may not): two-finger tap, two-finger scrub (= escape/back), three-finger tap (= repeat description), three-finger double-tap (= Zoom toggle), four-finger triple-tap (= Live Recognition).

---

### 16.3 Photos' user-authored custom Image Description (per-photo alt text)

Apple ships **user-authored alt text on individual photos**, buried in the info sheet. The iPhone User Guide flow (the `[button]` placeholders are inline SF Symbol glyphs that strip out of the HTML — an honest rendering, not a gap):

> "Add custom descriptions of images in Photos — Go to the Photos app… Double-tap the image you want to add a custom description to. Double-tap [button], then double-tap [button]. Double-tap [button], then double-tap Image Description. Enter your custom description."

And the payoff, verbatim:

> "After you add a custom description to a photo in the Photos app, you'll hear the description when you select the photo in the photo picker, and when you double-tap it."

So it is a per-asset accessibility description field persisted in the Photos library, surfaced by VoiceOver in Photos **and in the system photo picker**, taking precedence over auto-generated Image Descriptions.

**Pain points:** four double-taps deep through the info sheet; no bulk entry; almost nobody knows it exists.

⚠️ **Trap / needs physical-device + SDK audit:** **No documented PhotoKit API to read or write this field could be found.** `PHAsset` appears to have no public `accessibilityDescription` property. Treat programmatic read/write as **unavailable until proven otherwise** — meaning alt text a user typed in Apple Photos likely will **not** be visible to our app, and vice versa. **Someone must check `PHAsset` / `PHAssetChangeRequest` in the current SDK before we design our field.** If a read API does exist, our sync story changes materially (we could import users' existing alt text).

---

### 16.4 Accessibility > Motion — the toggles that gate photo autoplay

Settings > Accessibility > **Motion**, iOS 26. All seven toggles and their parentheticals below were verified word-for-word.

| Toggle | Apple's parenthetical |
|---|---|
| **Reduce Motion** | "Turn on. (When off, you'll see more motion, like the fluid morphing effects of Liquid Glass.)" |
| **Vehicle Motion Cues** | — |
| **Auto-Play Animated Images** | "Turn off. (When on, rapid animated images and moving elements such as GIFs in Messages and Safari play automatically.)" |
| **Auto-Play Video Previews** | "Turn off. (When on, it allows apps such as the App Store to automatically play video previews.)" |
| **Auto-Play Message Effects** | — |
| **Prefer Non-Blinking Cursor** | — |
| **Limit Frame Rate** | "Turn on. (On models with ProMotion display technology, this limits the maximum frame rate of the display to 60 frames per second.)" |

⚠️ **Trap:** **Dim Flashing Lights** and **Reduce Bright Effects** are **not** on the Motion page — they live under Accessibility > **Display & Text Size** (the Motion page merely routes you there). Users routinely cannot find them. Apple's on-device flashing detection, verbatim: "Your iPhone uses an on-device algorithm to detect flashing or strobing lights included in supported media and automatically dims them on your iPhone in real time."

**API surface, and the React Native gap:**

| Setting | Native iOS API | RN `AccessibilityInfo` binding? |
|---|---|---|
| Reduce Motion | `UIAccessibility.isReduceMotionEnabled`, `prefersCrossFadeTransitions` | ✅ `isReduceMotionEnabled()` (cross-platform); `prefersCrossFadeTransitions()` (iOS) |
| Auto-Play Video Previews | `UIAccessibility.isVideoAutoplayEnabled` + `videoAutoplayStatusDidChangeNotification` | ❌ **No RN binding — native module required** |
| Auto-Play Animated Images | Apple's animated-images accessibility doc | ❌ No RN binding |
| Reduce Transparency | `isReduceTransparencyEnabled` | ✅ |
| Bold Text | `isBoldTextEnabled` | ✅ (iOS) |
| Grayscale / Invert Colors / Darker System Colors | — | ✅ `isGrayscaleEnabled()`, `isInvertColorsEnabled()`, `isDarkerSystemColorsEnabled()` (iOS) |
| Android equivalents | — | ✅ `isHighTextContrastEnabled()`, `isAccessibilityServiceEnabled()`, `getRecommendedTimeoutMillis()` |

On Android, RN's `isReduceMotionEnabled()` reads the "Remove animations" / animator-duration-scale system setting.

Apple's HIG is explicit: "Avoid autoplaying audio and video content without also providing controls to start and stop it… consider global settings that let people opt out of auto-playing all audio and video," and links directly to `isVideoAutoplayEnabled`.

**Photos' own in-app autoplay toggle:**
- **macOS: confirmed verbatim.** Photos Settings > **General**: "**Autoplay Videos and Live Photos**: Set videos and Live Photos to play automatically when opened or when the pointer is placed over them."
- **iOS 26: UNVERIFIED.** Neither the researcher nor the fact-checker could source the current iOS label or location from any apple.com page. A search snippet suggested it moved into the Photos app (tap your account → a motion/loop toggle, possibly worded "Auto-Play Motion and Loop Videos"), but the underlying Apple page did not resolve for either pass. ⚠️ **Trap:** **Do not ship a UI string claiming iOS parity here.** This requires a **physical-device audit on iOS 26.5** before anyone writes the label. The fact-checker explicitly flagged that a later wave must not "fix" this by asserting a label.

Likewise: **whether Apple's Photos app gates Memories animation on Reduce Motion is not sourceable from apple.com.** The Reduced Motion evaluation criteria clearly impose that obligation on *us* (via the auto-advancing-carousel clause, §16.9), but do not assert it as a claim about Apple's behavior.

---

### 16.5 Display & Text Size — Dynamic Type, Bold Text, Smart Invert

#### 16.5.1 Larger Text / Bold Text / Dynamic Type

Settings > Accessibility > Display & Text Size:
- **Larger Text** — "Tap Larger Text, then drag the slider to adjust the text size. For additional text sizes, turn on Larger Accessibility Sizes."
- **Bold Text** — "Make text heavier: Turn on Bold Text."

**Apple's bar for claiming Larger Text support** (from the Larger Text evaluation criteria, verbatim):
> "You can indicate that your app supports Larger Text if users can enlarge text to at least 200% or the maximum font size for the system."
> "Dynamic Type on iOS, for example, reaches sizes larger than 200% at the AX3 size, and allows body text sizes over 300% at the AX5 size."
> "Don't rely on system-provided assistive technology like Zoom or Hover Text to claim support for Larger Text."

Failure modes Apple disallows: overlapping text, truncation to the point of ambiguity, clipping. The **Larger Text label is not offered on Mac.**

**Unverified sub-items:** the iOS 26 **"Show Borders"** setting and the Control Center **"Text Size"** slider were asserted by the researcher but the fact-checker could not source either to an apple.com page. **Treat both as unverified** — do not cite them as Apple UI.

**RN surface:** `Text` has `allowFontScaling` (**default `true`**), `maxFontSizeMultiplier`, `minimumFontScale`, `adjustsFontSizeToFit`, and iOS-only `dynamicTypeRamp` (default `'body'`; accepts `caption2`…`largeTitle`). Bold Text is readable via `AccessibilityInfo.isBoldTextEnabled()` (iOS) with a `boldTextChanged` event. **There is no RN API returning the raw Dynamic Type category**; `PixelRatio.getFontScale()` gives the multiplier.

⚠️ **Trap — the `maxFontSizeMultiplier` disqualifier:** RN teams reflexively set `maxFontSizeMultiplier` to stop layouts exploding. **Doing that caps scaling below 200% and disqualifies the app from declaring "Larger Text" in the Accessibility Nutrition Label.** The fix is layout reflow, not a font cap.

#### 16.5.2 Smart Invert vs Classic Invert — and the image exemption

Apple, verbatim:
- **"Smart Invert: Reverse colors everywhere except images."**
- **"Classic Invert: Reverse all the colors onscreen."**

Smart Invert's "except images" behavior **is not automatic — it is opt-in per view.** UIKit exposes **`accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors`** (iOS 11+); a view (and its subviews) with this set to `true` is exempted. Apple's own Photos sets it on photo content. **If you don't set it, your users' photos get color-inverted — faces turn blue.** This is the single most common visible a11y bug in third-party photo apps, and users notice instantly.

**RN support:** `accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors` is a documented **iOS-only View prop** (present in RN's `AccessibilityPropsIOS`). `isInvertColorsEnabled()` + `invertColorsChanged` are available in RN's `AccessibilityInfo` (iOS).

⚠️ **Trap / needs empirical check:** **expo-image's documented prop list does not mention `accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors`.** The corpus *infers* that wrapping the image in a plain `<View accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors>` works — because the UIKit property applies to the view subtree — but **this was not verified empirically.** Test Smart Invert against our actual image component before assuming.

**Also on the Display & Text Size page:**

| Setting | Note |
|---|---|
| **Color Filters** | Apple: "Note: Color filters can change the look of images and videos." **We cannot exempt photos from Color Filters** the way we can from Smart Invert. |
| **Reduce White Point** | — |
| **Reduce Transparency** | "Some backgrounds appear transparent or blurred by default… make these transparent backgrounds opaque." |
| **Differentiate Without Color** | Also a declarable Nutrition Label feature. |
| **On/Off Labels** | — |
| **Reduce Bright Effects** | iOS 26. |
| **Display Pulse Smoothing (PWM)** | Toggle is literally labeled "Display Pulse Smoothing (PWM)". "Display Pulse Smoothing is available on iPhone 17, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max, and iPhone Air." |
| **Dim Flashing Lights** | — |

### 16.6 Zoom, Voice Control, Guided Access, Per-App Settings

#### 16.6.1 Zoom

> "You can magnify the entire screen (Full Screen Zoom) or magnify only part of the screen with a resizable lens (Window Zoom). And, you can use Zoom together with VoiceOver."

**Options:** Follow Focus, Smart Typing, Keyboard Shortcuts, Zoom Controller, Zoom Region, **Zoom Filter** (None / Inverted / Grayscale / Grayscale Inverted / Low Light), Maximum Zoom Level; with a pointer: Zoom Pan and Adjust Size with Zoom.

**Gestures (system-owned; the app never sees them):** activate = **double-tap the screen with three fingers**; adjust magnification = three-finger double-tap-and-drag; pan = three fingers; Zoom menu = three-finger triple-tap.

Apple itself acknowledges the collision: "In many apps, you can zoom in or out on specific items. For example, you can double-tap or pinch to look closer in Photos."

**APIs (no RN bindings — native module needed for either):**
- `UIAccessibility.registerGestureConflictWithZoom()` — warns the user when the app's gestures conflict with Zoom (exists precisely for the three-finger conflict).
- `UIAccessibility.zoomFocusChanged(zoomType:toFrame:in:)` — tells Zoom where to look.

⚠️ **Trap:** Two-finger gestures (our pinch-to-change-grid-density and pinch-to-zoom in the detail view) survive. **Any three-finger gesture — e.g. a tempting three-finger "select multiple" shortcut — will be eaten by Zoom.** Do not ship one.

#### 16.6.2 Voice Control

> "When you're not sure what to call something, you can display a name or number next to each item on the screen… Say 'Show names,' 'Show numbers,' or 'Show text numbers.'"

Also **"Show grid"** for a numbered spatial grid, with drill-down. Overlay setting: "Display numbers, names, or a grid over screen elements." Voice Control requires a one-time offline file download. (⚠️ The phrasing "then works without internet" is a **paraphrase** — the download and offline language packs are documented; that exact claim is not on the Voice Control user-guide page.)

**Voice Control derives spoken names from accessibility labels.** An unlabeled element gets only a number, or nothing. In a photo grid, that means "Show numbers" yields a sea of numbered squares and selecting a specific photo by voice is near-impossible.

**Language support — 20 locales (iOS 26, `apple.com/ios/feature-availability`; matches item-for-item, including Apple's own inconsistent bare "Italian"):** Arabic (Saudi Arabia); Cantonese (China mainland); Cantonese (Hong Kong); English (Australia); English (Canada); English (India); English (United Kingdom); English (United States); French (France); German (Germany); **Italian**; Japanese; Korean; Mandarin Chinese (China mainland); Mandarin Chinese (Taiwan); Russian; Spanish (Mexico); Spanish (Spain); Spanish (United States); Turkish.

**API:** Voice Control consumes the same `accessibilityLabel` we set for VoiceOver, plus `accessibilityUserInputLabels` (UIKit) for alternate spoken names. ⚠️ **Trap: there is no RN binding for `accessibilityUserInputLabels`** — a native patch is required if we want short spoken aliases.

#### 16.6.3 Guided Access

> "With Guided Access, you can temporarily restrict iPhone to a single app… You can set a time limit, and customize which features, hardware buttons, and areas of the screen are available."

**Session Settings** (Apple's order): Side Button, Volume Buttons, **Motion** ("to prevent iPhone from switching from portrait to landscape or from responding to other motions"), Software Keyboards, Touch, Time Limit. You can also "Circle any areas of the screen you want to disable."

Apple's warning, verbatim: **"Important: Crash Detection and Emergency Services aren't available while using Guided Access."** (Contrast §16.1.1 — Crash Detection *does* keep working in Assistive Access.)

**APIs (no RN binding — native module):** `UIAccessibility.isGuidedAccessEnabled` + `guidedAccessStatusDidChangeNotification`; `requestGuidedAccessSession(enabled:completionHandler:)`; and app-defined restrictions via `configureForGuidedAccess(features:enabled:)` + `guidedAccessRestrictionState(forIdentifier:)`.

**Opportunity:** Guided Access alone does *not* stop an app's own destructive paths — apps must self-restrict. Apple Photos does not define custom Guided Access restrictions. We can.

#### 16.6.4 Per-App Settings

> "You can choose different color, text size, and motion settings for certain apps or for the Home Screen and App Library. Go to Settings > Accessibility > Per-App Settings. Tap Add App, then choose an app from the list (or Home Screen & App Library)."

(iOS 15+; current page title is "Customize visual accessibility settings for specific apps on iPhone". The Accessibility > Motion page cross-links to it, independently confirming that per-app overrides cover **motion** as well as color and text.)

The overrides arrive through the normal `UIAccessibility` state + trait-change channels — nothing to call, but we **do** have to respond to them.

⚠️ **Trap — do not cache accessibility state at launch.** A user can change *our app's* motion setting via Per-App Settings and come straight back. Reanimated's `useReducedMotion()` explicitly "returns a boolean indicating whether the reduced motion setting was enabled **when the app started**" — a launch-time snapshot, and therefore a stale-value bug in exactly this scenario. Subscribe to the live `AccessibilityInfo` events (`reduceMotionChanged`, `boldTextChanged`, `invertColorsChanged`, `screenReaderChanged`, `reduceTransparencyChanged`, `grayscaleChanged`) plus font-scale changes, and re-render.

#### 16.6.5 Hover Text is macOS-only

Hover Text is a **macOS** feature (System Settings > Accessibility > Hover Text), **not an iOS one.** Do not plan iOS Hover Text work — it does not exist there.

Confirmed settings: **Activation modifier**; **Triple-press modifier to set activation lock**; **Hover Typing**; **Hover Color**; configurable text size, font, and colors. Functionally, you move the pointer over something on screen (text, an input field, a menu item, or a button) and macOS displays a high-resolution zoomed version of it in a separate window.

⚠️ **Trap:** The corpus's original definitional sentence — "lets you zoom whatever is under the pointer—text, fields, menu items, buttons, and more—in high resolution in a separate window" — was **presented as verbatim but is a paraphrase**. **Do not ship it inside quote marks.** (Apple's actual "don't rely on it" line *is* verbatim: "Don't rely on system-provided assistive technology like Zoom or Hover Text to claim support for Larger Text.")

macOS reads text from the accessibility (AX) tree under the pointer. **If an app doesn't expose an AX tree, Hover Text shows nothing.** Electron apps are notorious for weak macOS AX trees — Hover Text and VoiceOver land on generic "group" nodes. Chromium only builds its accessibility tree when it detects assistive technology; Electron exposes `app.setAccessibilitySupportEnabled(enabled)` — "Manually enabling accessibility features… system assistive utilities take priority and will override this setting." Electron auto-enables when it detects e.g. VoiceOver on macOS; third-party AT can force it by setting `AXManualAccessibility` on the app's AXUIElement.

---

### 16.7 Enforcement: what actually gates us (it is not App Review)

#### 16.7.1 App Review does NOT enforce accessibility — a verified negative

The **App Store Review Guidelines (Last Updated: June 8, 2026)** were fetched live and searched by both the researcher and the fact-checker. Result: **ZERO hits for "VoiceOver," ZERO for "Dynamic Type," ZERO for "Nutrition Label," and no accessibility requirement anywhere in the document. Apps are not rejected by App Review for being inaccessible.**

⚠️ **Trap — the corpus's original word-counts were wrong, and a "verified negative" with wrong counts is worse than no count.** The corrected facts:
- **"accessibility" appears once in the guideline body** (not only in nav chrome) — in the app-collection rule: apps "recommending a collection of third-party apps that are designed for a specific approved need (e.g. health management, aviation, accessibility)".
- **"accessible" appears six times in the body** (not three), including "accessible for review" (metadata rule), the free-trial clause ("content or services that will no longer be accessible when the trial ends"), and the consent clause ("easily accessible and understandable way to withdraw consent").

The conclusion survives intact; the counts do not. Cite the conclusion, not the counts.

#### 16.7.2 …but App Review DOES police false accessibility *claims*

This is the step the original research stopped one short of. Apple:

> "make sure to follow App Review Guideline 2.3 for accurate metadata. If an app potentially has intentionally misleading or harmful accessibility labels, App Review has the ability to contact the developer and ask them to update their Accessibility Nutrition Labels."

**The enforcement surface is over-claiming in the label, not under-delivering on accessibility.** Declaring "Supports VoiceOver" when the pairing flow is unusable is the reviewable offense.

#### 16.7.3 Accessibility Nutrition Labels — the real bar

App Store Connect > **Manage App Accessibility**. The labels "help users learn if an app will be accessible to them before they download."

**Exactly nine declarable features:**

| # | Feature | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **VoiceOver** | |
| 2 | **Voice Control** | Not on Apple TV / Watch |
| 3 | **Larger Text** | "Increases the text size in the app to 200% or more"; **not offered on Mac** |
| 4 | **Dark Interface** | |
| 5 | **Differentiate Without Color Alone** | |
| 6 | **Sufficient Contrast** | |
| 7 | **Reduced Motion** | Note Apple's exact name: "Reduced Motion", not "Reduce Motion" |
| 8 | **Captions** | |
| 9 | **Audio Descriptions** | |

**The declaration bar, verbatim:**
> "To indicate support for an accessibility feature in the Accessibility Nutrition Labels, users must be able to complete all of the common tasks of your app using that feature."

**And Apple's definition of "common tasks," verbatim:**
> "Common tasks consist of the primary functionality that you expect users to perform in your app, plus functionality that's fundamental to using an app in general: first launch experience, login, purchase, and settings."

**Status:** "providing these labels will be voluntary to start… but over time, you'll be required to share accessibility support details to submit new apps and app updates to the App Store." **No published deadline exists.** Labels display on iOS/iPadOS/macOS/tvOS/visionOS/watchOS **26 and later**. Declaration is **per-device-family** (iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch).

#### 16.7.4 The user-generated-content carve-out — the most important clause in this whole domain

Apple, on the Nutrition Labels overview:

> "When third-party or user-generated content views are part of your common tasks, you don't need to ensure all third-party content is accessible, but your app should provide the third-party content creators a reasonable, discoverable way to make their content accessible."

With the on-point example:

> "In apps that allow users to upload images, developers should provide a way for the users to label the image, so the image content is perceivable to VoiceOver users."

**This reframes the entire VoiceOver-label workstream.** A photo app does **not** have to auto-describe every user photo to declare "Supports VoiceOver." It has to ship a **discoverable per-photo labeling affordance.** Auto-captioning is our *differentiator*, not our compliance obligation — which means we can declare the label before the ML is perfect, and it de-risks the whole program.

#### 16.7.5 The Accessibility URL field — the sanctioned escape hatch

Apple lets you link an **Accessibility URL** on the App Store product page, documenting partial support, in-app accessibility settings, caption languages, and explicitly "areas of your app that don't support an accessibility feature." This is the sanctioned way to support VoiceOver everywhere *except*, say, an editing canvas, without lying in the label.

#### 16.7.6 Other forcing functions

- **EU law.** The European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882) applies from 28 June 2025 and covers consumer ICT services in the EU, with EN 301 549 (which incorporates WCAG 2.1 AA) as the conformance route. ⚠️ **This is from secondary sources only** (accessibility vendors), not EUR-Lex. The scope-for-a-photo-app question, any per-country fine figures, and the "EN 301 549 v4.1.1 expected 2026" claim were **not** confirmed. Directionally right; **get counsel before putting numbers in a deck.**
- **Reputation.** The blind/low-vision community (AppleVis et al.) reviews photo apps publicly and loudly.

⚠️ **Trap:** Nobody on the team should claim "App Store review will reject us for this." It won't. Frame accessibility work as **label eligibility + EU market access + differentiation**, not as review risk.

---

### 16.8 Apple's VoiceOver evaluation criteria — the actual definition of "supports VoiceOver"

⚠️ **Trap — language hardening.** Apple writes **"should," "strive to," "we recommend," "consider"** throughout these criteria. The original research repeatedly rendered these as **"must,"** and four of its quotation-marked strings turned out to be **paraphrases, not Apple's words.** In a document used as a compliance gate, that manufactures obligations Apple did not state. The corrected quotations follow.

**Verbatim and correct:**
- Users "must be able to navigate and interact with visual elements, including text, media, buttons, and controls, using only VoiceOver."
- Users must "complete all of the common tasks of your app using only VoiceOver, without sighted assistance."
- "Ensure that labels don't include control types like 'checkbox' or states like 'checked'" — traits carry those; labels must be concise and make sense out of context.
- "If you can tap, click, or drag something in your app using a mouse or touchscreen gestures, you should strive to make it work with VoiceOver, too."
- Navigation must progress without skipping items or looping.
- Modals must trap focus and support `accessibilityPerformEscape()`.

**Corrected — these are Apple's actual words, not the paraphrases the researcher used:**

| Apple actually says | The paraphrase to NOT use |
|---|---|
| "**Most** images should include a relevant description or alternative text. If an image is purely decorative, make sure it's ignored completely by VoiceOver." | "Images should include relevant descriptions or alternative text; decorative images should be ignored by VoiceOver." (drops Apple's "Most" hedge) |
| "If your app provides a way for users to upload media, such as images, ensure users have a way to include labels or descriptions for the user-generated content…" | "User-generated media should support labels/descriptions." |
| "When content reloads or refreshes in the background, a VoiceOver user's reading position shouldn't reset unexpectedly." | "Content reloading/refreshing should not reset the VoiceOver cursor unexpectedly." |
| "Complex app behaviors, such as drag and drop or multi-touch gestures, **should** be provided in an accessible, discoverable way, such as through a custom rotor or action." | "…must be accessible through custom rotors or actions." |

**Two additional criteria the original research missed:**
- **Charts / data visualizations:** "Charts and other data visualizations should include accessibility information through a more specific chart API, or at minimum, include a reasonably complete text alternative." (Relevant to any stats, histograms, or face-cluster visualizations we ship.)
- **The duplicate-control exception, which is a gift for a dense photo grid:** "you might hide a button from VoiceOver in one view if it duplicates functionality that's already available and discoverable elsewhere." This *licenses* collapsing redundant per-cell controls rather than exposing every one.

**Two clauses are exactly where infinite-scroll photo grids fail:** VoiceOver reading-position reset on content refresh, and skipping/looping during virtualized navigation. See §16.10.

**RN implementation surface for these criteria:** `accessibilityLabel`, `accessibilityRole`, `accessibilityState`, `accessibilityValue`, `accessibilityActions` + `onAccessibilityAction`, `accessibilityViewIsModal`, `accessibilityElementsHidden`, `onAccessibilityEscape` (iOS), `importantForAccessibility` (Android), `experimental_accessibilityOrder` (Android).

---

### 16.9 Reduced Motion + Sufficient Contrast evaluation criteria — the numbers

**Reduced Motion criteria.** Disable or modify:
- Depth simulation — "parallax effects, animated blur, and depth-of-field effects"
- "multi-axis motion, multi-speed motion, spinning, or vortex effects"
- "auto-advancing carousel screens or any other ongoing motion" — stop them, or give a control to stop them

Distinguish **decorative** motion (stop entirely) from **meaningful** motion — replace the latter "such as a dissolve, highlight fade, or color shift." **Do not simply delete meaningful motion, or you delete the meaning.**

Apple's detection guidance: **"Detect when the user has the Apple system setting enabled"** and **"Avoid requiring users to manually configure a separate in-app setting. If offering in-app customization, provide similar or more granular functionality than the system setting."**

**Sufficient Contrast criteria (verbatim numbers):**
- **"4.5 to 1 between foreground text and its background"**
- **"Meeting a 3:1 minimum contrast ratio is commonly recommended for non-text contrast"** — interactive controls, non-text representations of state, icons
- Must hold in **both** light and dark, accounting for "translucency, opacity, and blurring."

⚠️ **Trap — the contrast test matrix is two passes, not one.** Apple says test **"with Increase Contrast on and Reduce Transparency off, and with both settings on."** Testing only "all settings on" misses the harder case.

**HIG, tappable-target size, verbatim:** "A button needs a hit region of at least **44x44 pt** — in visionOS, **60x60 pt**."

**Tooling:** Xcode's Accessibility Inspector uses WCAG AA values. UI-test automation exists: the correct symbol is **`performAccessibilityAudit(for:)` on `XCUIApplication`**, with the audit-type enum **`XCUIAccessibilityAuditType`** (WWDC23 session 10035, "Perform accessibility audits for your app"). ⚠️ "XCUIAccessibilityAudit" as a bare symbol name — as the original research wrote it — **is not a real symbol.** Android's equivalents: Espresso `AccessibilityChecks` and the Accessibility Scanner app.

⚠️ **Trap for a photo grid specifically:** a photo grid is the **worst contrast environment that exists** — white text over an arbitrary user photo, with no fixed background to contrast against. There is no way to verify contrast against user content. Any label rendered over a photo must sit on a scrim/plate with a guaranteed 4.5:1.

---

### 16.10 Making a virtualized photo grid accessible in React Native

This is the largest engineering item in the domain, and it is entirely on us.

#### 16.10.1 The verified negative: no RN list library ships any accessibility code

Both the researcher and the adversarial fact-checker **independently downloaded the published npm tarballs and grepped them.** The results reproduced exactly:

| Package | Version | Files | `/accessib/i` matches |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@shopify/flash-list` | 2.3.2 | 300 | **The only match is `dist/tsconfig.tsbuildinfo`** — a TypeScript build artifact, not source |
| `@legendapp/list` | 3.3.2 | 29 | **Zero** |
| `@react-native/virtualized-lists` | 0.86.0 | 30 | **Zero files contain `accessib`** |

None of them contains `accessibilityCollectionItem`, `accessibilityRole`, `accessibilityLabel`, or `importantForAccessibility` **anywhere.** `FlatList.js` on `facebook/react-native` main: zero `accessib` references. FlashList's official docs have no accessibility page; its "Known issues" page lists only RTL padding, horizontal-list headers, and data-reorder movement — nothing about screen readers.

⚠️ **Trap — one corpus claim was overstated and will not reproduce.** The researcher wrote that a GitHub issue search across `Shopify/flash-list` for VoiceOver / TalkBack / "screen reader" "returns no issues at all." **False as literally stated.** Re-running it: `repo:Shopify/flash-list` + TalkBack returns **three** hits (#1302, #959, #1023) — though all three are dependabot PRs bumping `react-native-gesture-handler` where "TalkBack" appears only in a pasted changelog, i.e. noise. VoiceOver = 0 and "screen reader" = 0 as claimed. In `LegendApp/legend-list`, VoiceOver returns **1** hit (#28, "Road to v1"), not zero. **The conclusion survives** — there are no genuine screen-reader bug reports in either repo — but do not repeat the "zero issues" phrasing. **Lean on the tarball grep; it is first-hand and far stronger evidence.**

#### 16.10.2 Why recycling is the hazard

FlashList: "When an item gets out of the viewport, instead of being destroyed, the component is re-rendered with a different item prop." FlashList **always** recycles. Legend List does **not** recycle by default (`recycleItems` prop opts in).

Recycling means the native view backing a cell is reused with new content — which is **precisely the condition under which a screen-reader cursor parked on that view can be silently re-pointed at different content, or lost.** This collides head-on with Apple's VoiceOver criterion: "When content reloads or refreshes in the background, a VoiceOver user's reading position shouldn't reset unexpectedly."

**What still works:** item-level accessibility. Cells are ordinary RN components, so `accessible`, `accessibilityLabel`, `accessibilityRole`, `accessibilityActions` all function inside `renderItem`. **What is missing is everything list-level and collection-level.**

#### 16.10.3 React Native removed list collection semantics

In 2022, commit **`463af237539b98289c88e5b491c85cbf53bcaf0c`** (2022-08-03) landed, titled exactly: *"TalkBack support for ScrollView accessibility announcements (list and grid) - Javascript Only Changes (#33180)"*. Its message reads, verbatim:

> "Javascript logic in the FlatList, SectionList, VirtualizedList components to provide accessibility information (row and column position) for each cell in the method renderItem as a fourth parameter accessibilityCollectionItem. The information is saved on the native side in the AccessibilityNodeInfo and announced by TalkBack when changing row, column, or page."

**That code is no longer present.** Verified first-hand against `@react-native/virtualized-lists` 0.86.0 and `facebook/react-native` main. RN's current `ViewAccessibility.js` contains 83 accessibility references but **no collection props at all**:
- **Android props:** `accessibilityLabelledBy`, `aria-labelledby`, `accessibilityLiveRegion`, `aria-live`, `importantForAccessibility`, `screenReaderFocusable`
- **iOS props:** `accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors`, `accessibilityViewIsModal`, `accessibilityShowsLargeContentViewer`, `accessibilityLargeContentTitle`, `aria-modal`, `accessibilityElementsHidden`, `accessibilityLanguage`, `accessibilityRespondsToUserInteraction`

⚠️ **Trap — cite the commit, not the PR.** GitHub reports PR **#33180** as `state=closed, merged=FALSE, merged_at=null`. Meta landed it through their internal import ("Pull Request resolved: https://github.com/facebook/react-native/pull/33180"). Saying "PR #33180 added X" is substantively right, but a reader who opens the PR page will see it as unmerged and conclude we fabricated it.

**Consequence:** modern RN emits **no** `AccessibilityNodeInfo.CollectionInfo` / `CollectionItemInfo` for FlatList/VirtualizedList. On Android, `accessibilityRole="grid"` / `"list"` maps to a **className hint only** — it does **not** populate collection counts and indices. Every RN photo grid on Android today announces photos as an undifferentiated stream with **no position**: no "row 3 of 200," no "column 2 of 4." In a 40k-photo library, that is total disorientation.

Android's own platform made this manual too: per the RecyclerView release notes, `CollectionInfo` / `CollectionItemInfo` are no longer populated by default and "you will need to populate them yourself if you want Accessibility Services like Talkback to indicate count and item index to the user."

**To get real TalkBack collection announcements you must reach native:** set `AccessibilityNodeInfoCompat.CollectionInfo` on the scroll container and `CollectionItemInfo` (row, column, rowSpan, colSpan) on each cell via a custom `AccessibilityDelegate`.

#### 16.10.4 Reanimated + Reduce Motion: a bug class that makes photos INVISIBLE

Reanimated respects reduced motion via the `ReduceMotion` enum (`System` = default, `Always`, `Never`), the `ReducedMotionConfig` component, and `useReducedMotion()`. Documented behavior when reduced motion is on: "entering, keyframe, and layout animations instantaneously reach their endpoints. Exiting animations and shared transitions are omitted," and `withSpring` / `withTiming` "return the toValue immediately."

**But the library has repeatedly shipped bugs where the short-circuit leaves opacity/transform at the *initial* (invisible) value instead of the endpoint — so the view never appears at all.** All four issue numbers below were verified against the GitHub API in `software-mansion/react-native-reanimated` (the fact-checker noted this was the area he most expected fabrication and found none):

| Issue | Title | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **#6987** | "Views with `entering` animations never appear when reduced motion is active" | created 2025-02-06, closed |
| **#8046** | "Entering animations not completing if Reduce Motion accessibility setting is on (v3.19)" | closed 2025-08-26 |
| **#9771** | "Entering animation leaves view invisible under Reduce Motion on iOS **(with ENABLE_SHARED_ELEMENT_TRANSITIONS disabled)**" | closed 2026-06-26 |
| **#9615** | "[Bug] Reduced Motion always reduce example crashes on iOS" | closed 2026-06-11 |

Recurring across 3.16 → 3.19 → 4.x. ⚠️ Note that **#9771's parenthetical materially narrows the repro** — the original research truncated the title without an ellipsis, which overstates the bug's breadth.

⚠️ **Trap:** This is the worst possible accessibility outcome — **a user turns ON an accessibility setting and the app's photos become invisible.** It has shipped repeatedly. Treat it as a release-blocking test, not a nice-to-have.

⚠️ **Trap:** `useReducedMotion()` "returns a boolean indicating whether the reduced motion setting was enabled **when the app started**." It is a **launch-time snapshot**, and iOS Per-App Settings let a user change our app's motion setting and come right back (§16.6.4).

#### 16.10.5 Android: TalkBack already auto-describes images, so a lazy label just looks mediocre

Google shipped on-device image description in TalkBack. From the Android Developers Blog (**dated September 2024**, Android 15 Spotlight Week):

- "TalkBack automatically provides users with blindness or low vision more vivid and detailed image descriptions thanks to Gemini Nano with multimodality."
- "The average TalkBack user comes across **90 unlabeled images per day**."
- It replaced an older small model ("Garcon") that "produced short, generic responses."
- "Using an on-device model like Gemini Nano was the only feasible solution for TalkBack to provide automatically generated detailed image descriptions for images, even while the device is offline."
- There is also a cloud-backed path — "combining the strengths of both Gemini Nano on device and Gemini 1.5 Flash in the server."

⚠️ The corpus's device scoping ("TalkBack 15.x+ / Pixel-class devices") is an **inference not stated in that post** — do not present it as sourced.

**The dynamic is symmetric with iOS Image Descriptions: the OS papers over our missing labels with a generic auto-caption.** Which means a lazy implementation **does not look broken — it looks mediocre**, and we silently lose our differentiation. The OS captioner knows "a dog on a blanket." It does not know the people, the place, or the date. We do.

Android's accessibility-principles doc additionally requires: `collectionInfo` / `collectionItemInfo` (with rowCount/columnCount), `contentDescription = null` for decorative images, `onLongClickLabel` for long-press actions, `mergeDescendants` for grouping, and custom actions for swipe/drag gestures. **None of it is free.**

#### 16.10.6 The implementation checklist for our grid

1. **Every cell:** `accessible={true}`, `accessibilityRole="imagebutton"`, a full `accessibilityLabel` (our generated description + date + people), and `accessibilityActions` for favorite / share / delete / select.
2. **List container:** `accessibilityRole="grid"` (RN's role enum includes both `'list'` and `'grid'`) — but understand this is a **className hint on Android and populates no indices.**
3. **Announce position ourselves.** No library will do it. Either (a) ship a native Android `AccessibilityDelegate` that stamps `CollectionInfo` / `CollectionItemInfo` on the grid — correct, invisible to users, matches platform behavior; or (b) bake "row 3, column 2, item 47 of 12,940" into each cell's `accessibilityLabel` — cheap, verbose, and TalkBack reads it in the wrong idiom. **Do (a) if we're serious about Android parity; do (b) only as a stopgap.** Either way, this **does not come with FlashList** and must be budgeted.
4. **Test the recycling × cursor interaction explicitly.** Park VoiceOver/TalkBack on a cell, scroll programmatically, confirm the cursor does not jump or read stale content.
5. **Consider `recycleItems={false}` on Legend List when a screen reader is active**, eating the perf cost — screen-reader users scroll slowly, so the perf argument for recycling largely evaporates. ⚠️ **This is an inference, not sourced guidance.** Neither library documents an accessibility mode. It follows from how recycling works, but **nobody has published it and it must be validated with a real VoiceOver/TalkBack scroll test before we build on it.**
6. **Never remount the list on data change.** Make updates additive and stable-keyed. Our grid re-renders constantly (sync lands new assets from the desktop, ML backfills labels, thumbnails resolve) — each one is a chance to yank the VoiceOver cursor back to the top of a 40,000-photo library.
7. **Expose multi-select drag and swipe-to-delete as `accessibilityActions`**, never gesture-only.
8. **44x44 pt hit regions** on every photo-cell overlay button even when the visible glyph is smaller — trivially violated in a dense 4-column grid.

---

### 16.11 What this means for us

#### Requirements (do these or we are broken / disqualified)

| # | Requirement | Why |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | **Set `accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors` on every surface rendering actual photo/video content** — grid cells, detail viewer, people thumbnails, memory covers, share previews, desktop-sync preview. Do **not** set it on chrome (chrome *should* invert). | Cheapest, highest-visibility fix in the domain. Without it, Smart Invert turns every face blue. Verify it actually forwards through **expo-image** — this is unverified. |
| R2 | **Every photo cell carries an `accessibilityLabel`.** A bare unlabeled image falls back to Apple's generic captioner (or TalkBack's Gemini Nano) and we lose our differentiation silently. | §16.2.1, §16.10.5 |
| R3 | **Ship a discoverable per-photo labeling affordance**, and an `accessibility_description` field in the asset schema — distinct from `caption`/`title`, user-editable, auto-populated from our captioner with an explicit `auto` vs `edited by you` provenance flag, and **carried across the E2E LAN sync protocol** so a description written on the phone appears on the desktop. | This is literally Apple's UGC carve-out requirement (§16.7.4) and their VoiceOver criterion for uploaded media. Apple does not sync alt text outside iCloud — we can. |
| R4 | **Gate autoplay on BOTH Reduce Motion AND Auto-Play Video Previews.** RN gives us the first; the second needs a **native module** wrapping `UIAccessibility.isVideoAutoplayEnabled` + `videoAutoplayStatusDidChangeNotification`, and on Android reading `Settings.Global.ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE`. | Our grid autoplays Live Photos and our Memories animate. |
| R5 | **Our in-app autoplay toggle DEFAULTS to the system state, never overrides it, and is MORE granular than Apple's** (separate "motion in grid" / "motion in detail view" / "Memories playback"). | Apple's Reduced Motion criteria: "Detect when the user has the Apple system setting enabled" and "Avoid requiring users to manually configure a separate in-app setting. If offering in-app customization, provide similar or more granular functionality than the system setting." |
| R6 | **Never cache accessibility state at launch.** Subscribe to live `AccessibilityInfo` events + font-scale changes. Do **not** trust Reanimated's `useReducedMotion()` as source of truth. | Per-App Settings (§16.6.4) makes launch-time snapshots a live bug. |
| R7 | **Release-blocking CI gate: run the app with Reduce Motion forced ON** (`<ReducedMotionConfig mode={ReduceMotion.Always} />` in a test build, or the simulator setting) and **assert photos actually render.** Snapshot/screenshot test that catches invisible views. Pin and track the Reanimated version against #6987 / #8046 / #9771 / #9615. | Our grid cells, lightbox, and the 13-primitive love-touch micro-interaction system all use entering/layout animations. This bug class ships repeatedly. |
| R8 | **Let text scale unbounded — do NOT set `maxFontSizeMultiplier`.** Instead reflow: reduce grid columns (4→2→1) at large accessibility sizes, move date/section headers to full-width rows, let names wrap. Keep repeated chrome (Back, Edit) smaller as Apple advises. Use `dynamicTypeRamp` on iOS. Honor Bold Text via `isBoldTextEnabled()`. | Capping the multiplier caps scaling below 200% and **disqualifies us from declaring "Larger Text."** |
| R9 | **Any label over a photo sits on a scrim/plate with guaranteed 4.5:1.** Selection state is never color-only — add a checkmark shape. All overlay buttons get 44x44 pt hit regions. | We cannot verify contrast against arbitrary user content. The checkmark also earns "Differentiate Without Color Alone." |
| R10 | **Under Reduce Motion:** our FLIP/shared-element lightbox zoom is *meaningful* motion → replace with a cross-fade, don't just cut it. Our Memories auto-advancing playback is literally Apple's "auto-advancing carousel" case → stop it or expose a stop control. Our "vivid living background" becomes static or cross-fading. And **Limit Frame Rate means we cannot assume 120Hz** for our "buttery" motion. | §16.9. Our maximalist design direction is on a direct collision course with both Reduced Motion and Sufficient Contrast. |
| R11 | **Assistive Access: detect it (`AccessibilitySettings.isAssistiveAccessEnabled`) and never gate the UI on an un-grantable permission prompt.** Degrade to a large, clear, non-dead-end "ask your supporter to enable Photos access" state. **Remove the LAN E2E pairing flow entirely from the AA scene** — it needs Local Network permission and a QR/code exchange, neither of which can happen in AA. Sync must be pre-configured by the supporter outside AA. | §16.1.1. This is a crash-class bug, not a polish item. |
| R12 | **Treat the desktop-pairing flow, semantic search, face naming/merging, NSFW review, and index-all-photos consent as first-class accessibility surfaces.** | Nutrition Labels bar = "**all** of the common tasks," and Apple defines common tasks to include first launch and settings. A beautiful VoiceOver grid is worthless if the QR pairing screen is unusable. |
| R13 | **Electron desktop:** render photo metadata and controls as real semantic DOM (button / role / aria-label), not divs; expose `app.setAccessibilitySupportEnabled` behind a user preference; wire `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-contrast`, and `nativeTheme`. Accept Chromium's AX-tree perf cost. | Without an AX tree, macOS Hover Text and VoiceOver see generic "group" nodes. The same living-background hazard applies on desktop. |
| R14 | **Adopt Apple's testing methodology verbatim as our QA gate.** Compile the main tasks per screen; build a matrix {iPhone, iPad} × {VoiceOver, Voice Control, Switch Control} × {Reduce Motion, Larger Text AX5, Bold Text, Smart Invert, Increase Contrast, Reduce Transparency, Differentiate Without Color} + an **Assistive Access row**; turn settings on **one at a time**; complete tasks using **only** each assistive technology. Contrast must be tested **twice** (Increase Contrast on / Reduce Transparency off, then both on). Wire `performAccessibilityAudit(for:)` (XCUITest) and Android Espresso `AccessibilityChecks` into the existing `qa.yml` so contrast/label/target-size regressions fail CI. | It is literally the same bar as the Nutrition Labels. Include a German (long-word) and an RTL language in the Dynamic Type snapshot matrix. |

#### Opportunities (where we can beat Apple)

- **Identity-rich descriptions.** We run CLIP-style semantic embedding, face recognition, and cross-age matching on the desktop node. Apple's captioner says "possibly, a black dog on a blanket." We can say **"Ana and Dad at the beach, October 2023"** — searchable, persistent, in languages Apple's 12-language Image Descriptions doesn't cover, with **no cloud.** This is the single strongest wedge in the domain.
- **Sensitivity warnings that mirror Apple's.** Our NSFW/Safe-Mode classifier already flags sensitive content. Announce the warning **before** the description, matching Apple's own behavior: "VoiceOver lets you know if an image has sensitive content before it describes the image."
- **A strictly better Explore Image.** We have exact face bounding boxes *and identities*. Drag your finger and hear **"Ana, top left" / "Dad, center"** — named people, not "a person." No competitor has this. Requires a shared native "accessible photo canvas" component on both platforms (§16.2.4).
- **OCR at ingest.** Adding `VNRecognizeTextRequest`-class OCR to the desktop pipeline gives us accessible photo text, OCR-backed semantic search ("find the receipt from the hardware store"), and coverage in the languages Apple's 8-language Text Recognition lacks. Expose recognized text in the detail view as separately-focusable VoiceOver elements in reading order (mirroring Apple's receipts/nutrition-labels behavior).
- **Voice Control gets real names for free.** Because every cell carries a generated label, a Voice Control user says **"Tap Ana at the beach"** instead of "Tap 47." (Consider a native patch for `accessibilityUserInputLabels` to add short spoken aliases — no RN binding exists.)
- **Assistive Access with one more capability.** Apple's AA Photos is camera-roll + shared albums only: no search, no people, no memories, no favorites. Ship an AA scene that mirrors Apple's exact vocabulary (**"Include Shared Albums," "Pinch to Zoom"** — so supporters recognize them) and adds a supporter-curated **People scope backed by our local face recognition**. That is meaningfully better, not just parity. Minimum viable first step: set `UISupportsFullScreenInAssistiveAccess=YES` (trivial Info.plist key via Expo config) to get the full frame instead of a letterboxed small-phone frame.
- **Custom Guided Access restrictions.** Use `guidedAccessRestrictionState(forIdentifier:)` to define our own restrictions — "Deleting photos," "Sharing photos," "Viewing sensitive content," "Desktop pairing" — so a supporter can hand over the phone with photos browsable but destructive/sensitive paths hard-disabled. **Apple Photos does not do this.** Small native module; high trust payoff.
- **Zoom focus following.** Call `zoomFocusChanged(zoomType:toFrame:in:)` when our lightbox opens so the Window Zoom lens follows the photo the user just opened. Almost nobody does this, and it makes our shared-element lightbox actually usable under Zoom. (Native module — no RN binding.)
- **Be an early, honest Nutrition Label declarer.** Realistic first-wave declarations: **VoiceOver, Larger Text, Dark Interface, Sufficient Contrast, Differentiate Without Color Alone, Reduced Motion, Voice Control.** Captions and Audio Descriptions concern video content we don't author — likely N/A. Use the **Accessibility URL** field to honestly document any surface that doesn't yet support a feature. On a photo app, this is free marketing on the product page — and thanks to the UGC carve-out (§16.7.4) we can declare VoiceOver on the strength of a *labeling affordance*, before the auto-captioner is perfect.

#### Items requiring a physical-device or SDK audit (do not guess)

1. **iOS 26.5 Photos in-app autoplay toggle** — exact label and location. Both research passes failed to source it. Do not ship a parity string until someone checks a real device.
2. **`PHAsset` / `PHAssetChangeRequest` in the current SDK** — is there any public read/write for the per-photo custom Image Description? If a read API exists, we can import users' existing alt text and our sync story changes materially.
3. **`accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors` through expo-image** — does it forward? Test Smart Invert against our actual image component. The `<View>`-wrapper workaround is an untested inference.
4. **`recycleItems={false}` when a screen reader is active** — validate with a real VoiceOver and TalkBack scroll test before building on it.
5. **Whether any Android OEM ships an Assistive Access equivalent** — entirely un-researched.
6. **European Accessibility Act scope for a photo app** — secondary sources only. Get counsel.
## 17. Child Safety & On-Device Content Moderation

This section covers the layer of iOS that sits *between* a photo and a person's eyes: Apple's two nudity-detection switches (Sensitive Content Warning for adults, Communication Safety for children), the `SensitiveContentAnalysis` (SCA) framework that exposes that capability to third parties, the Screen Time restriction that can permanently sever a third-party app from the photo library, and the Hidden-album lock that makes part of the library structurally invisible to us. The single most important thing to know: **SCA is not a library-scanning engine and cannot be used as one** — it returns a bare boolean, it silently returns *nothing at all* on a default adult device, and Apple explicitly forbids transmitting its verdicts off the device. Our own ONNX classifier (`crossage_fr/ingest/safety.py`) is not a fallback; it is the only architecture that works. The second most important thing: a Screen Time restriction can put our app into `PHAuthorizationStatus.restricted`, a terminal state with no in-app remedy — and our React Native permission library currently throws that signal away before it reaches JS.

---

### 17.1 The two OS switches that gate everything

Every third-party sensitive-content capability on iOS is gated behind one of exactly two user/parent settings. Nothing else un-gates SCA.

| | **Sensitive Content Warning (SCW)** | **Communication Safety** |
|---|---|---|
| Audience | Adults (and anyone) | Children in a Family Sharing group (Child Account required) |
| Settings path | Settings → Privacy & Security → Sensitive Content Warning | Settings → Screen Time → [child] → Communication Safety |
| Availability | iOS 17+ / iPadOS 17+ / watchOS 10+ / macOS Sonoma+ / visionOS 2+ | Messages: iOS 15.2+. All other supported apps: iOS 17+ |
| Default state | Off. ⚠️ **Not stated by Apple.** Strongly implied (the support page is written entirely as "Turn on Sensitive Content Warning"; the Personal Safety guide calls it optional), and Google states the parallel default explicitly — but Apple never says it in so many words. Treat as inferred. | **On by default for children under 18** on iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple Watch. For children 13–17, on by default on Apple Vision Pro. Explicitly stated by Apple, twice. |
| Behavior | Blurs photos/videos that may contain nudity before viewing; offers help resources | Warns, blurs, and offers resources when a child **receives OR attempts to send** nudity |
| Extra gate | — | For children **under 13**, a parent/guardian must enter the Screen Time passcode to view flagged content. Starts in iOS 18 / iPadOS 18 / macOS Sequoia / visionOS 2. |
| Reporting to Apple | Offered only for **an iMessage or FaceTime video call** detection. That path *does* send the content to Apple. | Same scoping. |

**Apple's app-coverage lists** (from HT105071 for SCW — verbatim, per device):
- **iPhone / iPad:** Messages, AirDrop, shared photo albums, Contact Posters in the Phone app and the Contacts app, and FaceTime calls and video messages.
- **Mac:** Messages, Contact Posters in the Phone app and the Contacts app, and shared photo albums.
- **Apple Watch:** Messages, Contact Posters, FaceTime video messages.
- **Apple Vision Pro:** Messages and AirDrop.

Turning SCW on enables it automatically for all supported apps, but Apple says "you can manage access for each app."

**Communication Safety's coverage** (HT105069) is the same set **plus one clause that matters more than anything else in this section**: it also intervenes *"when your child selects a photo or video to share in some third-party apps."* Apple lists that third-party hook on **iPhone/iPad, Mac, AND Apple Vision Pro** — not iPhone-only.

Apple's stated privacy property, for both features: *"Sensitive Content Warning uses on-device machine learning to analyze photos and videos. Because they're analyzed on your device, Apple doesn't receive an indication that nudity was detected and doesn't get access to the photos or videos as a result."* Enabling SCW on iPhone also enables it on the paired Apple Watch.

> ⚠️ **Trap:** Apple's own **Personal Safety User Guide** (published October 2025) is **stale** — it lists only "Messages, in AirDrop, in a FaceTime video message, and in the Phone app when receiving a Contact Poster," omitting shared photo albums and the Contacts app. **HT105071 is authoritative** (page footer: "Published Date: March 24, 2026"). This is a live example of a broader rule for this whole domain: Apple's child-safety documentation is internally inconsistent right now. Cross-check every claim against two pages.

---

### 17.2 What Apple protects inside Photos — and the gap it leaves

Apple Newsroom, **June 11, 2025**, announcing iOS 26's child-safety release, verbatim:

> "Communication Safety expands to intervene when nudity is detected in FaceTime video calls, and to blur out nudity in Shared Albums in Photos."

This **is shipping today** (released with iOS 26 in fall 2025; current shipping OS is iOS 26.5.2). Also confirmed in that same June 2025 article: kids 13–17 get age-appropriate protections "from the beginning, regardless of whether their account was set up as a Child Account or a standard Apple Account" (including web content filters and Communication Safety); the **PermissionKit** framework for parent-approved new contacts; and App Store age ratings expanded to five categories with three adolescent tiers — **13+, 16+, and 18+**.

> ⚠️ **Trap:** Apple's word is **"intervene."** The widely-repeated "freezes FaceTime video" description is *press* language (MacRumors/iDropNews), not Apple's. Do not put "Apple freezes FaceTime" in comparison copy.

**The gap.** Apple has now explicitly drawn its line at ***shared*** content in Photos. Shared Albums are protected. **The user's own local camera roll is not classified by Apple at all** — not by SCW, not by Communication Safety, not on any shipping OS. That gap is precisely where our Safe Mode lives.

---

### 17.3 SensitiveContentAnalysis — the framework, and why it cannot be our engine

**Entitlement:** `com.apple.developer.sensitivecontentanalysis.client`, added via the **Sensitive Content Analysis capability** in Xcode. Apple, verbatim: *"Any team member of the paid App Store developer program can add the entitlement to an app after enabling the capability in Xcode and then signing the Developer Program License Agreement on the website. The Sensitive Content Analysis entitlement isn't available for Enterprise development or for people with free accounts."*

**Framework availability:** iOS 17.0+ / iPadOS 17.0+ / Mac Catalyst 17.0+ / macOS 14.0+ / visionOS 2.0+.

| Class / API | What it does | Real availability |
|---|---|---|
| `SCSensitivityAnalyzer.analyzeImage(_:)` | Analyzes an in-memory image (`CGImage`) | iOS 17+ |
| `SCSensitivityAnalyzer.analyzeImage(at:)` | Analyzes an image at a file URL | iOS 17+ |
| `SCSensitivityAnalyzer.videoAnalysis(forFileAt:)` → `hasSensitiveContent()` | Analyzes a video **file**; the returned `SCSensitivityAnalyzer.VideoAnalysisHandler` carries a `progress` property | iOS 17+ |
| `SCSensitivityAnalyzer.analysisPolicy` | The gate (see below) | iOS 17+ |
| `SCSensitivityAnalysis.isSensitive` (`Bool`) | The **entire** result. No probability, no score, no threshold, no fine-tuning, not open source, Apple platforms only. | iOS 17+ |
| `SCVideoStreamAnalyzer` | Analyzes a **live** stream (`AVCaptureDeviceInput` or `VTDecompressionSession`) | ⚠️ **iOS 26.0 / iPadOS 26.0 ONLY** — no macOS, no Mac Catalyst, no visionOS |

> ⚠️ **Trap (corrected from a common misreading):** `SCVideoStreamAnalyzer` is **not** an iOS 17 API. Live-stream nudity analysis is brand-new, iPhone/iPad-only, and iOS 26+. Any cross-platform plan that assumed it reached back to iOS 17 or existed on macOS is wrong.

> ⚠️ **Trap:** `shouldIndicateSensitivity`, `shouldInterruptVideo`, and `shouldMuteAudio` are **not callbacks** on `SCVideoStreamAnalyzer`. They are **properties on the `SCSensitivityAnalysis` result object**, delivered through the single `analysisChangedHandler` callback.

`SCVideoStreamAnalyzer`'s initializers throw if the user has both settings off — Apple, verbatim: *"The initializers of this class throw an error if both settings are off."*

#### The gate: `analysisPolicy == .disabled` has three distinct causes

The framework detects **nothing** — silently, with no error — under **any** of:

1. The app lacks the `com.apple.developer.sensitivecontentanalysis.client` entitlement.
2. **Neither** Sensitive Content Warning **nor** Communication Safety is active.
3. One of the sensitive-content detection settings *is* active, **but the person turned off sensitive-content warnings for your app specifically in Settings.** (Apple: *"One of the sensitive content detection settings is active, but the person turned off sensitive-content warnings for your app in Settings."*)

> ⚠️ **Trap:** Cause (3) means a global `SCW = on` does **not** guarantee your app gets analysis. **Check `analysisPolicy` on every call; never cache it.** And because SCW is off by default for adults, on a typical adult device SCA returns `.disabled` and yields nothing at all — which is trivially mistaken for "no sensitive content found." That is a dangerous false-negative failure mode. There is **no API to ask the user to enable SCW from inside your app.**

#### The purpose limit — Apple's exact words

From the setup article ("Detecting nudity in media and providing intervention options"), in an *Important* callout:

> "Apple provides the Sensitive Content Analysis framework to prevent people from viewing unwanted content, not as a way for an app to report on someone's behavior. To protect privacy, don't transmit any information off the person's device about whether the Sensitive Content Analysis framework identified an image or video as containing sensitive content."

Apple's framing throughout is **pre-display interdiction of externally-sourced/incoming media** — its own examples are a messaging app checking each received image, a classroom app checking uploads, a video-conferencing app checking participant streams.

#### The definitive verdict on bulk library scanning

**Apple publishes no sentence prohibiting library scanning.** Any claim of an explicit written ban is fabricated — do not repeat one. But SCA is nonetheless **categorically unusable** as a library-scanning engine, for four independent reasons: it is user-opt-in-gated and silently returns nothing on a default adult device; it is purpose-limited to pre-display protection rather than behavioral reporting; it returns a bare boolean with no score; and it forbids exporting detection results off the device. Both the "Apple explicitly bans it" answer and the "SCA is a sanctioned bulk-scan tool" answer are wrong.

---

### 17.4 ⚠️ Trap: Apple's SCA docs contradict themselves on the policy enum

This is a **live documentation bug in Apple's own reference** (present as of July 2026) that will silently invert any implementation that trusts the wrong page.

| Page | Says `simpleInterventions` means… | Says `descriptiveInterventions` means… |
|---|---|---|
| `SCSensitivityAnalyzer.analysisPolicy` property page — **WRONG** | "someone activates the **Communication Safety** parental control in Screen Time" | "someone activates the **Sensitive Content Warning** user preference" |
| `SCSensitivityAnalysisPolicy.simpleInterventions` / `.descriptiveInterventions` enum-case pages — **CORRECT** | "the person turned on … **Sensitive Content Warnings** user preference" + "Keep the intervention minimal … consider blurring and annotating the area … versus raising a new fullscreen alert" | "the person turned on … **Communication Safety** parental control in Screen Time" + "Use child-appropriate language" + "Present an alert that fills the full screen." |

It is **2-against-1**, not a coin flip. Two further sources side with the enum-case pages: (a) the `SCSensitivityAnalysisPolicy` enum overview page's own code sample (`else if policy == .simpleInterventions { // The Sensitive Content Warning setting is active. } else if policy == .descriptiveInterventions { // The Communication Safety setting is active. }`); and (b) the setup article's prose — keep interaction brief and unobtrusive for adults; for children, use the full view and age-appropriate language. The semantics agree too: *simple* = terse adult inline blur; *descriptive* = the overt, explanatory child flow.

**Consequence of getting it backwards:** you show a terse, easily-dismissed inline blur **to children** and a full-screen, child-worded modal **to adults** — precisely inverting the safety design and failing the vulnerable population. **Implement from the enum-case pages. Never from the `analysisPolicy` page.** If we ever touch SCA, pin a code comment explaining why.

---

### 17.5 `detectedTypes` / gore & violence — iOS 27 only, NOT shippable

`SCSensitivityAnalysis.detectedTypes` exposes the specific categories present, via `SCSensitivityAnalysis.ContentType`: documented values include **`.sexuallyExplicit`** and **`.goreOrViolence`**.

**Platform badges on both `detectedTypes` and `SCSensitivityAnalysis.ContentType`: iOS 27.0 BETA / iPadOS 27.0 BETA / Mac Catalyst 27.0 BETA / macOS 27.0 BETA / visionOS 27.0 BETA.** iOS 27 was announced at WWDC on **June 8, 2026** and is in developer/public beta; GA expected ~September 2026. **Current shipping iPhone OS is iOS 26.5.2. Do not plan a shipping feature on this, and do not put it on a near-term roadmap as available.**

Apple Newsroom (June 8, 2026), verbatim: *"Communication Safety already blurs nudity when detected in Messages and FaceTime calls, and is turned on by default for users under 18, and now it will also intervene to block gore or violent content when detected in shared images or videos."* And, dispositively on shipping status: *"New features will be available after installing the Screen Time update in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27."* That same Newsroom article explicitly points third-party developers at **SensitiveContentAnalysis**, **PermissionKit**, and the **Declared Age Range API**.

Semantics, verbatim from Apple: *"The framework populates this set only when `isSensitive` is true"* and *"Your app can continue to use `isSensitive` alone if you don't need to differentiate between content categories."*

**Apple's interaction research is stealable regardless of whether we adopt SCA.** Its sample code branches: `showContentWarning(allowAccess: true)` for `.sexuallyExplicit` (reveal after acknowledgment) versus `blockContent(...)` for `.goreOrViolence` (hard block). Its stated rationale, verbatim: *"Because violent imagery can be traumatic on immediate exposure, progressive reveal interfaces—such as sliders that gradually remove blur—give people greater control over their exposure."*

> ⚠️ **Trap:** Apple's setup article **silently mixes iOS 17 and iOS 27 APIs in a single code sample with no availability badge on the page.** `detectedTypes` appears unannotated. Anyone copy-pasting Apple's own sample will write code that **fails to compile against a shipping SDK.**

---

### 17.6 Apple's SCA test harness — a QR code that forces a guaranteed false positive

Apple ships a documented way to exercise the full sensitive-content intervention flow **without ever handling real sensitive material**.

| Asset | URL |
|---|---|
| Test image | `https://developer.apple.com/sample-code/web/qr-sca.jpg` |
| Test video | `https://developer.apple.com/sample-code/web/qr-sca.mov` |
| Config profile | `https://developer.apple.com/services-account/download?path=/iOS/iOS_Logs/SensitiveContentAnalysis.mobileconfig` |
