Install `SensitiveContentAnalysis.mobileconfig` on the dev device and **reboot** ("Reboot the device for the test profile to take effect"). With the profile active, analyzing media containing the QR code returns `isSensitive == true` (and, on iOS 27, `detectedTypes` containing `.sexuallyExplicit`). Apple: *"the analyzer … returns a false positive for this QR code for the special purpose of testing."* The QR code can be embedded inside larger host media at varying size and position — *"the framework can still recognize it if its details remain crisp and unobstructed"* — and **in a video file it must be in the first frame.** Apple's stated rationale is letting you experience the intervention workflow "in an open development environment, or while demonstrating the app to an audience."

**The pattern is stealable even though we won't adopt SCA.** See 17.13.

---

### 17.7 The Screen Time Photos lock — the permanent-library-loss failure mode

**This is the highest-value single finding in this section for our RN app.**

Apple's parental-controls documentation lists the restriction with this exact label:

> **"Photos: Prevent apps from requesting access to your photos in the Photos app"**

Navigation path (confirmed verbatim): Settings → **Screen Time** → under **Family**, tap your child's name → **Content & Privacy Restrictions** → (enter Screen Time passcode) → under **Privacy**, tap **Photos**.

**How it manifests to a third-party app:**

- `PHPhotoLibrary.authorizationStatus(for: .readWrite)` returns **`PHAuthorizationStatus.restricted`**.
- Apple's definition of that case is exact: *"The app isn't authorized to access the photo library, and the user can't grant such permission."*
- `requestAuthorization` presents **no system prompt** and resolves immediately as `.restricted`.
- Deep-linking the user to our app's Settings page is **futile** — the Photos row is locked.
- The state does not change until whoever holds the Screen Time passcode changes it.

**Detection:** check for `.restricted` **explicitly** and treat it as a **terminal, non-recoverable state distinct from `.denied`**. Do not retry. Do not re-prompt. **Do not offer "Open Settings."**

There is **no API** to request removal of the restriction, **no API** to detect who set it, and **no API** to prompt the passcode holder. `PHPhotoLibrary.authorizationStatus(for:)` is the entire read surface.

> ⚠️ **Trap:** The most common implementation — a generic "grant photo access in Settings" screen — is **the single worst thing to do here.** It sends the user on a dead-end errand to a greyed-out toggle with no explanation. Apple Community threads show even sophisticated users cannot work out why apps can't see their photos, and there are reports of the Photos restriction toggle behaving buggily / reverting.

> **Needs a physical-device audit:** The two option labels on the Photos row — widely reported as **"Allow Changes" / "Don't Allow Changes"** — are corroborated only by third-party write-ups and Apple Community threads. Apple's HT105121 describes the restriction in prose and gives the navigation path but does not show the labels; the iPhone User Guide article bodies are JS-rendered and could not be extracted. **Read these off a real device before putting them in shipping UI copy.**

---

### 17.8 ⚠️ Trap: `react-native-permissions` destroys the `.restricted` signal at the bridge

**We are currently blind to the Screen Time lock in our stack.** Verified by reading `master` source (not docs; library is actively maintained — default branch `master`, last push 2026-06-16, ~4.4k stars, 7 open issues).

In `ios/RNPermissions.mm`, `stringForStatus` maps native status to the JS `RESULTS` strings:

```objc
case RNPermissionStatusNotAvailable:
case RNPermissionStatusRestricted:
  return @"unavailable";
```

| Native status | JS `RESULTS` string |
|---|---|
| `RNPermissionStatusNotAvailable` | `unavailable` |
| `RNPermissionStatusRestricted` | `unavailable` ← **collision** |
| `RNPermissionStatusNotDetermined` | `denied` |
| `RNPermissionStatusDenied` | `blocked` |
| `RNPermissionStatusLimited` | `limited` |
| `RNPermissionStatusAuthorized` | `granted` |

The PhotoLibrary handler (`ios/PhotoLibrary/RNPermissionHandlerPhotoLibrary.mm`) **does** correctly read `PHAuthorizationStatusRestricted → RNPermissionStatusRestricted` from `[PHPhotoLibrary authorizationStatusForAccessLevel:PHAccessLevelReadWrite]`. **The information is captured natively and then thrown away at the bridge.**

Two bugs fall out:

1. A parent-locked photo library is **indistinguishable at the JS layer** from "this permission has no handler / isn't supported on this device" — both are the literal string `unavailable`. A real user ends up seeing "not supported on this device" when in fact their parent turned off Photos in Screen Time.
2. The idiomatic RN recovery flow keys off `RESULTS.BLOCKED` to show "you denied us, open Settings" — which **never fires** for the restricted case, and would be **useless if it did**.

> ⚠️ **Trap (naming):** In this library, `RESULTS.DENIED` means **not-yet-asked / requestable** — *not* "the user said no." "User said no" is `RESULTS.BLOCKED`. Teams routinely get this backwards.

**Fix options:** (a) ship a thin native module that calls `PHPhotoLibrary.authorizationStatus(for: .readWrite)` and returns the five `PHAuthorizationStatus` cases verbatim to JS (cheap; leaves the dependency untouched); or (b) patch/fork `react-native-permissions` to emit a distinct `restricted` result. Without one of these, 17.7's requirement is **literally unimplementable in our stack** — the signal never reaches JS.

---

### 17.9 The Hidden album is structurally invisible to us

PhotoKit reference for `PHAssetCollectionSubtype.smartAlbumAllHidden`, verbatim: hidden assets — *"the system doesn't return them through a fetch request, by default"* — and the key sentence:

> "Beginning with iOS 16, users can require authentication to view the hidden Smart Album, and the user setting is true by default. When true, the system returns an empty Smart Album."

Apple support confirms: *"In iOS 16, iPadOS 16.1, and macOS Ventura and later, your Hidden album is locked by default and requires authentication to unlock in Photos."* Unlockable with Face ID, Touch ID, or passcode. The user can change this at **Settings → Apps → Photos** (which holds both "Show Hidden Album" and the Use Face ID / Use Touch ID / Use Passcode lock toggles).

**What we get back is an empty collection — not an error, not a permission prompt, just nothing.** There is **no way for a third-party app to authenticate the user and unlock it**; that is a first-party Photos capability only. Recently Deleted is locked by the same mechanism.

---

### 17.10 The Android mirror

**The permission lock: `DevicePolicyManager.setPermissionGrantState`.** Callable only by a **profile owner, device owner, or a delegate holding `DELEGATION_PERMISSION_GRANT`**. With `PERMISSION_GRANT_STATE_DENIED`, AOSP states verbatim: *"Runtime permission state: The permission is denied to the app and the user cannot manage the permission through the UI."* Also: *"Note that user cannot manage other permissions in the affected group through the UI either and their granted state will be kept as the current value."*

Applied to `READ_MEDIA_IMAGES` / `READ_MEDIA_VIDEO`, this permanently denies our app the photo library with no user-side remedy — **the exact Android equivalent of `PHAuthorizationStatus.restricted`.** Note the Android S+ "restricted sensors" carve-out (location / camera / mic / body sensors, plus HealthPermissions on BAKLAVA), which a profile owner may deny but not grant, **does not include the media permissions** — so `READ_MEDIA_IMAGES` / `READ_MEDIA_VIDEO` are freely deniable by a profile owner and this failure mode is fully live. `getPermissionGrantState` exists but is callable only by the admin, not by us.

**Detection (there is no direct `.restricted` equivalent — you must infer):** `checkSelfPermission` returns `PERMISSION_DENIED`, **AND** `shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale` returns `false`, **AND** a runtime request resolves immediately with no visible dialog. That triad means *either* permanently-denied-by-user *or* admin-locked. On a managed / Family Link device, assume the latter. ⚠️ **Trap: the ambiguity is inherent to Android and cannot be fully resolved** — the UI copy must honestly cover both cases.

**The classifier: Android System SafetyCore.** Google Messages' "Sensitive content warnings" detect and blur images that may contain nudity, warning on **receive, send, and forward**. Google, verbatim: *"All detection and blurring of nude images happens on the device. This feature doesn't send detected nude images to Google."* / *"Sensitive content warnings use SafetyCore to perform classification on devices and doesn't send identifiable data or any of the classified content or results to Google servers."* / *"As a system service, SafetyCore is only active when an application integrates with SafetyCore and specifically requests content to be classified."* / *"This feature doesn't currently work on videos."*

User path: Google Messages → profile picture → Messages settings → Protection & safety → Manage sensitive content warnings → "Warnings in Google Messages".

**Google's age-tiered defaults** (more explicit than Apple's, and the better-reasoned model):

| Cohort | Default | Can turn off? |
|---|---|---|
| Supervised users | **On** | **No** — parents control it via the Family Link app |
| Unsupervised teens (13–17) | **On** | Yes, in Google Account settings |
| Adults (18+) | **Off** | — |

> **UNVERIFIED — do not plan on it:** Google describes SafetyCore only as "common infrastructure that apps can use." **No public, documented, generally-available third-party classification API was found on developer.android.com** equivalent to Apple's SensitiveContentAnalysis. All authoritative material is user-facing (Google Messages help, Family Link help). Treat "third parties can call SafetyCore" as unverified.

---

### 17.11 App Store Review Guidelines 1.1.4 / 1.2 — what actually binds us

**Guideline 1.2 (User-Generated Content)** requires apps with UGC or social networking services to include, verbatim:

- "A method for filtering objectionable material from being posted to the app"
- "A mechanism to report offensive content and timely responses to concerns"
- "The ability to block abusive users from the service"
- "Published contact information so users can easily reach you"

Apps whose UGC ends up primarily pornographic *"do not belong on the App Store and may be removed without notice."*

**Guideline 1.1.4** covers overtly sexual or pornographic material, defined as *"explicit descriptions or displays of sexual organs or activities intended to stimulate erotic rather than aesthetic or emotional feelings."*

> ⚠️ **Trap (this exact clause has been mis-quoted before, with the load-bearing part cut off):** 1.2's incidental-NSFW carve-out reads — *"If your app includes user-generated content from a web-based service, it may display incidental mature 'NSFW' content, provided that the content is hidden by default and only displayed when the user turns it on **via your website**."* **The opt-in must live on your website, not behind an in-app toggle.** Implementing from the truncated version (an in-app "show NSFW" switch) is not what the guideline authorizes and would sink a review.

**Scope test for us:** 1.2 attaches to content *posted to the app / to a social service*. Our app is local-first with no cloud account, and LAN sync moves the user's **own** photos between the user's **own** two devices — that is not UGC posted to a service. **1.2 most likely does not attach today.**

---

### 17.12 The CSAM precedent — and the corrected read of the 2026 climate

Apple announced client-side CSAM detection (NeuralHash — hashing images against a known-CSAM database on the path to iCloud Photos) in **August 2021**, paused it after backlash, and formally dropped it in **December 2022**, stating *"Children can be protected without companies combing through personal data."* In its **August/September 2023** response to the Heat Initiative, **Erik Neuenschwander** (Apple's director of user privacy and child safety) argued that scanning every user's privately stored iCloud data *"would create new threat vectors for data thieves to find and exploit,"* would *"inject the potential for a slippery slope of unintended consequences,"* and that *"scanning for one type of content … opens the door for bulk surveillance."* Apple pivoted to Communication Safety instead — which is exactly why SCW/Communication Safety are architected as **pre-display, on-device, non-reporting** features. That architecture is scar tissue, not accident.

> ⚠️ **Sourcing caveat:** **None of these Apple statements were ever published on apple.com.** Both the Dec 2022 statement and the 2023 Heat Initiative letter were given to WIRED and are only available press-mediated. They are real and correctly attributed, but they **cannot be cited to a primary Apple URL** — treat as press-attested, not Apple-published.

**CORRECTED — do not adopt the "the wind has reversed" thesis.** Legal pressure on Apple to *reinstate* detection is actively **intensifying**, not settled: the ~2,680-victim class action in N.D. Cal. (filed December 2024, seeking ~$1.2B) is **still live**, and on **February 19, 2026** West Virginia Attorney General **John McCuskey** sued Apple seeking damages and **injunctive relief requiring Apple to implement effective CSAM detection** (contrasting Google's ~1.47M reports in 2023 with Apple's ~267). Positioning our local NSFW classifier on "the backlash settled the question in favor of no scanning" would be **building on contested ground.**

**What is durable is the lexical lesson, not the political one.** The public heuristic that hardened in 2021 is crude but durable: *"an algorithm looking at my photos" = surveillance.* It does not distinguish local classification from server-side reporting. Any messaging that trips that heuristic loses, regardless of our actual architecture.

---

### 17.13 What this means for us

**A. Keep our own ONNX classifier. This is now positively validated, not merely tolerated.**
Three independent disqualifiers rule SCA out as our Safe Mode engine: (1) it returns `.disabled` and yields **nothing** on a default adult device, so our core feature would silently not work for most users; (2) it returns **no score**, while `crossage_fr/ingest/safety.py` is built on `score` / `threshold` / `level` / `category_scores` and our entire threshold-profile + temperature-calibration + folder-calibration design depends on a continuous score; (3) it is Apple-only, and there is **no cross-platform first-party alternative** — Google's SafetyCore has no confirmed public API. Our own classifier is the only way to get consistent, scored, cross-platform Safe Mode behavior.

**B. HARD RULE — no Apple-derived safety verdict ever crosses the LAN wire.**
Apple: *"don't transmit any information off the person's device about whether the Sensitive Content Analysis framework identified an image or video as containing sensitive content."* Our desktop is **a different device**. "It's E2E-encrypted and it's the user's own Mac" is an argument *we* would be making, not one Apple has made — Apple has not addressed this case. ⚠️ **This is an interpretation, not a sourced fact**, and the conservative reading costs us nothing: if we ever adopt SCA for any secondary purpose, its verdicts stay on the phone. **All cross-device safety state must be OURS.** The same rule forbids logging SCA verdicts to analytics, crash reports, or any accuracy-monitoring pipeline.

**C. LAUNCH BLOCKER (iOS): build the native permission shim.**
Ship a thin native module returning all five `PHAuthorizationStatus` cases verbatim to JS. Without it, `.restricted` is invisible to our JS layer (17.8) and the correct error message is unimplementable. Then write the empty/blocked-library state **once, cross-platform**, handling **three** cases:

| State | iOS signal | Android signal | Copy / recovery |
|---|---|---|---|
| Not yet asked | `.notDetermined` | `checkSelfPermission` denied + rationale **true** (or never asked) | Prompt normally |
| User denied (recoverable) | `.denied` | denied + rationale true | Offer **Open Settings** |
| **Administratively locked (terminal)** | **`.restricted`** | denied + rationale **false** + request resolves with no dialog | **Never offer "Open Settings."** Name the real lever: *"Photo access is turned off by Screen Time. Ask whoever manages Screen Time on this iPhone to open Settings → Screen Time → Content & Privacy Restrictions → Photos and allow changes."* On Android, name the device administrator or Family Link, and honestly cover the permanently-denied-by-user case too. |

Because our value proposition is reading the whole camera roll, the terminal state means the app is fundamentally non-functional on that device — **degrade gracefully** to whatever still works (desktop-side library, already-synced items) rather than showing a hard wall.

**D. Child accounts: we are the one unguarded photo surface on the phone.**
Our app takes **full `PHPhotoLibrary` access and renders its own grid**, which means we deliberately bypass the system photo picker — and therefore bypass Communication Safety's third-party hook. ⚠️ **This bypass is an inference, not documented.** Apple's word is "*some* third-party apps" and it does not specify the mechanism; it reads like the PHPicker path, but Apple never says whether a full-library app escapes it. **This must be validated on a real supervised device.** It determines whether forcing Safe Mode on for child accounts is an obligation or merely well-advised.

Regardless of the outcome, the safe design: **detect a supervised/child context and force Safe Mode ON and non-disableable there.** Consider routing share/export flows through `PHPickerViewController` specifically so the OS intervention still fires for free (no entitlement required). Use the **Declared Age Range API** (announced June 2025, reiterated June 2026) to request the age range associated with a Child Account **without learning the birth date**, and adapt our safety UI accordingly.

**E. Adopt Google's default matrix, which is better reasoned than Apple's.**
Supervised = **forced on, cannot be disabled**. Teen 13–17 = **on by default, can be turned off**. Adult 18+ = **off by default**. This makes "on by default for minors" defensible rather than paternalistic, and it mirrors both platforms' first-party behavior.

**F. Copy the interaction vocabulary; do not invent one.**
Users already recognize **blur + a one-word "Show" affordance + a secondary "get help" action** from SCW. Mirror it exactly. Steal Apple's category-specific research for free: **acknowledge-then-reveal for sexually explicit, hard-block by default with a progressive/slider reveal for gore/violence** (Apple: *"Because violent imagery can be traumatic on immediate exposure, progressive reveal interfaces—such as sliders that gradually remove blur—give people greater control over their exposure."*). And note App Store 1.2 independently corroborates the right default: flagged content **hidden by default, revealed only on explicit user action.**

**G. Adopt the Hidden-album mental model as our Safe Mode target state.**
Apple's Hidden album shows us the user's existing mental model: sensitive material belongs in a **locked place, gated by biometrics** — not merely blurred. That is the model our Safe Mode should adopt for anything it flags: a **biometric-gated vault**, the natural home for NSFW-positive items.

**H. Truth in advertising — we can never index the Hidden album.**
Hidden assets return an **empty** collection to us, and there is no third-party unlock path. **Never claim "all your photos" or "your entire library."** Users *will* notice hidden photos missing from search results. Say **"everything except your Hidden album"** and explain why it's a feature, not a bug. Bonus: our LAN sync protocol inherits this for free — hidden assets cannot leak to the desktop because we can never read them.

**I. Build a deterministic sentinel fixture, copying Apple's QR-code harness pattern.**
Add a synthetic marker image that our ONNX safety path is wired to score as **maximally sensitive under a dev/QA flag**, so that e2e tests, CI, tester-checklist runs, and — critically — **live demos of Safe Mode** never touch real intimate imagery. Wire it into `crossage_fr/ingest/safety.py` behind the same env-flag mechanism the module already uses. Given this repo already ships an NSFW/intimate-image classifier and a tester checklist, the **absence of such a sentinel is a standing operational and legal hazard for the team.**

**J. Ship gore/violence months before Apple.**
`.goreOrViolence` does not exist on any shipping iPhone OS — until iOS 27 GA (~Sept 2026) there is **no first-party gore/violence signal on iPhone at all, for anyone.** Our classifier already emits multi-category `category_scores` and a `level` (neutral/low/medium/high), so adding a gore/violence category is a model-and-threshold problem for us, not a platform problem. We can ship it **on iOS 26 today, on Android, and on the desktop**, with continuous scores Apple will still not provide.

**K. Positioning — three non-negotiable rules.**
1. **LEXICAL: never use the word "scan."** Apple's own postmortem made "scanning" the trigger word for "bulk surveillance," and the public heuristic does not distinguish local classification from server-side reporting. Say our app **"sorts," "organizes," or "classifies"** — and always name the beneficiary and the boundary in the same breath.
2. **ARCHITECTURAL HONESTY: do NOT say "on-device."** Our pipeline offloads ML from the phone to the user's own desktop over the LAN, so "on-device" is **literally false**, and getting caught overclaiming here would be a self-inflicted version of exactly what burned Apple. The accurate — and still excellent — claim is **"on your own devices — your phone and your Mac, over your own network. No cloud, no account, nothing is ever reported to anyone."**
3. **STRUCTURAL:** adopt the four properties that make local classification defensible and that Apple's critics specifically demanded — **no hash database of anyone else's content; no report path to any third party** (our no-cloud-account design already guarantees this); **user-visible and user-correctable verdicts** (our folder-calibration UI and pluggable explainer framework are exactly this — lead with them); and **a real off switch.** Our Safe Mode design already satisfies all four; the work is to *say* so, prominently, in-product and in App Review notes.

**Corollary: never add telemetry to Safe Mode.** Any detection signal leaving the user's devices collapses the entire position. Do not build a Safe Mode A/B test or accuracy-monitoring pipeline that phones home.

**L. Treat "no UGC surface" as an architectural invariant.**
We are almost certainly out of App Store 1.2's scope today. The moment we add **any** sharing surface, social feature, or server-mediated content exchange, 1.2 attaches and we inherit four hard obligations (filter, report, block, published contact) plus ongoing content-moderation liability. **Flag any future sharing feature as triggering a 1.2 review.** The latent asset: if we ever *do* add sharing, our Safe Mode classifier already **is** the "method for filtering objectionable material" 1.2 demands — we'd be the rare app satisfying that requirement locally, with no moderation backend.

**M. Differentiation claim we have actually earned.**
Apple guards *shared* content in Photos (Shared Albums, iOS 26) and never classifies the user's own local camera roll. Say it precisely — use Apple's exact term **"Shared Albums"**, and do **not** claim Apple "freezes" FaceTime (Apple says "intervene"). Our line: **"Apple guards what other people send you; we also guard what's already in your library, and we do it without a cloud account."**

---

### 17.14 Open questions requiring a physical-device or further audit

| Question | Status | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| The two option labels on the Screen Time → Privacy → Photos row ("Allow Changes" / "Don't Allow Changes") | **Unverified.** Corroborated only by third-party write-ups and Apple Community threads; Apple's own pages describe the restriction in prose only. | We must not ship UI copy quoting Apple UI labels we haven't read off a device. |
| Does a full-`PHPhotoLibrary`-access app bypass Communication Safety's third-party hook entirely? | **Inference, not documented.** Apple says "*some* third-party apps" and never specifies the mechanism. | Determines whether forcing Safe Mode on for child accounts is an obligation or merely advisable. **Validate on a real supervised device.** |
| Can **MDM** (not Screen Time) lock the per-app Photos permission? | **Unverified — and the premise may be wrong.** Every key in Apple's Device Management `Restrictions` payload (`com.apple.applicationaccess`) was enumerated and **no key locks the Photos per-app privacy permission**; the only Photo-related keys are `allowCloudPhotoLibrary` and `allowPhotoStream`, which are different things (iCloud Photos and Photo Stream). The payload has ~24 `allow*Modification` lock keys but none for Photos privacy. On current evidence the lock is a **Screen Time / Content & Privacy Restrictions** mechanism, not a dedicated MDM restriction key. | ⚠️ **Do not tell users "your IT administrator may have done this via MDM"** without verifying against Apple's Device Management reference. |
| Is Sensitive Content Warning off by default for adults? | **Inferred, not stated by Apple.** | Affects how we describe Apple's baseline in comparison copy. Confident, but hedge. |
| Does Apple's "off the person's device" rule cover the user's own paired Mac? | **Apple has not said.** Apple plainly had cloud/server exfiltration in mind. | We adopt the conservative reading (never sync SCA verdicts) because it costs us nothing. |
| Is there any public third-party SafetyCore classification API on Android? | **None found on developer.android.com.** | Reinforces (does not change) the decision to keep our own ONNX classifier. |
## 18. Photos Beyond the iPhone — Watch, TV, Vision Pro, Mac, Windows

Apple Photos is not one app; it is a constellation of surfaces whose third-party permeability is roughly inverse to how much users love them. The most-loved ambient surfaces (the Photos watch face, the Apple TV screen saver) are the most sealed — there is no third-party watch-face design API and no third-party tvOS screen-saver API — while the surfaces Apple neglects (Windows, iCloud.com, and arguably tvOS itself) are wide open because Apple ships almost nothing there. The single most important thing an implementer must know: **the Mac is the only platform where Apple's own face-analysis output is readable by us** (the `Photos.sqlite` `ZPERSON`/`ZDETECTEDFACE` tables), and **Windows is the largest greenfield in the entire domain** (Apple ships a file-sync client and zero photo intelligence). Build the curation engine surface-agnostically on the desktop; treat every other device as a thin presentation client fed over our own transport.

---

### 18.1 Apple Watch — the sync model (all content is pushed from the iPhone)

The watch has no photo library of its own and **`PHPhotoLibrary` is not available on watchOS at all**. Everything is a subset pushed from the paired iPhone. Configuration lives entirely in the iPhone's **Watch app > My Watch > Photos**.

| Apple UI label | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Sync Album** | Pick exactly one album to sync to the watch. The watch Photos app initially shows the **Favorites** album. |
| **Sync Memories** | Toggle: push Memories to the watch. |
| **Sync Featured Photos** | Toggle: push Featured Photos to the watch. |
| **Photo Syncing** | Master toggle. Turning it off stops syncing Memories, featured photos, *and* the chosen album. |
| **Photos Limit** | Caps how many photos are stored on the watch, to save space for songs and other content. |

All five labels are verbatim from Apple's Apple Watch User Guide page *"Choose a photo album and manage storage on Apple Watch."*

⚠️ **Trap:** The commonly-cited **Photos Limit** values **25 / 100 / 250 / 500** are **not Apple-documented**. Apple's own guide says only: *"The number of photos stored on your Apple Watch depends on available space."* The numeric set comes from third-party blogs (iDownloadBlog, OSXDaily), and the "500 is the maximum" framing directly contradicts Apple's language. **Unverified — do not ship these numbers as an Apple-sourced fact.** A physical-device audit is required to confirm what the picker actually offers.

⚠️ **Trap:** Apple's watch sync is **album-scoped, never person-scoped**. There is no "sync photos of my kid" primitive. Apple's own Photos-watch-face doc has to warn users: *"If you're not seeing photos, make sure the photos are in your synced album."*

**Third-party equivalent:** none for the system sync set — an app cannot write into it. The supported pipe is `WCSession.transferFile(_:metadata:)` (iOS 9.0+ / watchOS 2.0+; abstract: *"Sends the specified file and optional dictionary to the counterpart."*), which transfers files in the background from our iPhone app to our watchOS app.

⚠️ **Trap:** `transferFile` **does not work in the Simulator**. Testing this path requires paired physical hardware — budget for it.

---

### 18.2 Apple Watch — the on-watch Photos app

A pure viewer over the pushed subset. No search, no editing, no People browsing, no way to jump to a specific photo — you scroll.

| Interaction | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Content shown | Memories, Featured Photos, or the synced album, in a grid |
| Tap | Open a photo |
| Swipe left/right | Move between photos |
| Digital Crown | Zoom. *"Zoom all the way out to see the entire photo album."* |
| Drag | Pan |
| Double-tap | Toggle fill-screen vs. whole-image |
| Touch-and-hold | Play a Live Photo |
| Action button | Share |

Every element above is confirmed against Apple's *"View photos on Apple Watch."* All of it is fully replicable by a third-party watchOS app over its own image cache using public SwiftUI + Digital Crown rotation + gesture APIs.

---

### 18.3 Apple Watch — the Photos and Portraits watch faces

**Photos face.** Content sources, with Apple's exact wording:

- *"Shuffle your photo library: Tap Shuffle, tap Featured or People"*
- *"Shuffle a collection: Tap Shuffle, tap Collection, choose an album"*
- *"Manually add photos: Tap Choose Photos, select up to 24 photos"*
- *"When you shuffle your photo library or a collection, sixteen photos are automatically selected to display each day."*
- *"A new photo appears every time you raise your wrist or tap the display."*
- Apple's Face Gallery blurb also lists a Memory as a source: *"Choose an album, Memory, or up to 24 custom photos."*

⚠️ **Trap (structural, easy to get wrong):** an album is not a peer option to Shuffle — you pick it **inside Shuffle > Collection**. And the **16-photos-per-day rule applies only to shuffling** (library or collection), *not* to a manual 24-photo selection.

**Portraits face** (introduced watchOS 8). Apple's watchOS 8 newsroom post: the face *"brings to life stunning portrait photos shot on iPhone with an immersive, multilayered effect, intelligently recognizing faces in photos and cropping in to highlight the subject."* The subject is composited over the time; the clock layers between subject and background.

⚠️ **Trap — the "Portrait-mode capture required" claim is REFUTED.** Widely repeated in the press, but Apple's user guide says: *"The Portraits watch face uses photos from the photo library on your iPhone. Layer effects are applied to photos of people, dogs, cats, and landscapes."* Landscapes and pets are supported; it is **not** restricted to Portrait-mode captures of people. Do not design a competitive claim around "Apple requires captured depth" — that premise is wrong.

Confirmed Portraits details: up to 24 photos, three type styles, Digital Crown zoom, new photo on wrist-raise or tap. The setup path string *"Watch app > Face Gallery > Portraits > Content > Choose Photos…"* is **not verbatim in Apple docs — unverified**.

**A path the docs actually give you:** you can create a **Photos, Portraits, or Kaleidoscope** watch face **directly from the Photos app** — a shipping photo→face route that involves no developer API at all.

---

### 18.4 Apple Watch — can a third-party app put photos on a watch face? (the honest answer)

**No.** There is no third-party watch-face design API on watchOS.

The one real API is `CLKWatchFaceLibrary.addWatchFace(at:completionHandler:)` — abstract exactly *"An object for importing watch faces that the app provides"*; availability **iOS 14.0+ / iPadOS 14.0+ / Mac Catalyst 14.0+ / watchOS 7.0+**; **not deprecated**. It takes a local URL to a `.watchface` file and installs it with user confirmation. WWDC20 session 10100 (*"Meet Watch Face Sharing"*): *"Watch face files contain all the face's configurations, including color, styles, photos and complications, anything you can configure on a watch."*

⚠️ **Trap — do not read this as a photo-delivery API.** Apple's own article *"Sharing an Apple Watch face"* describes only **pre-authored, bundle-embedded** faces: you configure a face on a real watch, export the `.watchface` file, then *"drag both the .watchface file and the preview into Xcode to add them to the app's bundle"*, and *"Only add watch faces in response to the user tapping an Add Apple Watch Face button."* Apple also states the app must already be published to the App Store (the App Store Connect ID is embedded), and there is a `faceNotAvailable` error for faces the target watch cannot run (so ship fallback faces for older hardware).

**There is NO supported way to synthesize a `.watchface` at runtime containing the user's own photos.** The format is an undocumented zip (metadata.json + resources) reverse-engineered only by community tools such as `banjun/WatchFaceDumper`. This is reverse engineering, not an API. It is the single biggest open question in this research area and **requires a hardware spike before anyone promises it** — treat it as a 1-engineer-week prove-or-kill, never as a committed roadmap item.

⚠️ **Trap (platform risk):** **ClockKit complications are deprecated in watchOS 10+** (WidgetKit is the replacement). `CLKWatchFaceLibrary` survives, but the framework around it is in maintenance mode. Betting on `.watchface` import is betting on a maintenance-mode framework.

(The corpus's earlier claim that "Apple has publicly defended that choice" was **unsourced and dropped by the fact-checker** — do not repeat it.)

---

### 18.5 Apple Watch — what a third-party app *can* actually do (all four confirmed)

| Capability | API | Availability |
|---|---|---|
| Present a Photos picker on the watch | `PhotosPicker` (SwiftUI / PhotosUI) | iOS/iPadOS/Mac Catalyst 16.0+, macOS 13.0+, **watchOS 9.0+** |
| Enumerate / observe the photo library on the watch | `PHPhotoLibrary` | **NOT AVAILABLE on watchOS.** Listed for iOS 8+, macOS 10.13+, tvOS 10+, visionOS 1.0+, Mac Catalyst 13.1+ — watchOS is absent |
| Background file transfer phone→watch | `WCSession.transferFile(_:metadata:)` | iOS 9.0+ / watchOS 2.0+ |
| Render an image on the watch face / Smart Stack | WidgetKit accessory widgets & complications | Current |

⚠️ **Trap:** PhotoKit's *framework* page lists watchOS 10.0 — that is because `PhotosPicker` lives under PhotosUI. **It does not mean the library is enumerable on the watch.** Architect as `desktop ML → phone → transferFile → watch cache`, never as "the watch reads the library."

⚠️ **Trap (rendering):** WidgetKit's `WidgetRenderingMode` documents **`fullColor`** and **`accented`** as the modes used by watchOS complications (the desaturated **`vibrant`** mode is the iPhone Lock Screen). Whether your complication shows a full-colour photo depends on the watch face and the user's settings — on `accented` faces it will be tinted/flattened. Test every complication asset in `accented` mode and handle `WidgetAccentedRenderingMode` for images; design a graceful fallback (e.g. a segmented silhouette rather than a full photo).

### 18.6 Apple TV — the screen saver (Aerials / Snoopy / Memories & Slideshows / Portraits)

Category is chosen at **Settings > Screen Saver > Current Selection**. While a screen saver is running, swipe/press **up** to switch category.

| Category | Sub-settings (Apple's labels) |
|---|---|
| **Aerials** | *Choose Aerials* with themes **Cityscape, Earth, Landscape, Underwater**; **Download Frequency**; per-aerial hide and **Hide All** |
| **Snoopy** | Requires **Apple TV 4K (2nd generation) or later** |
| **Memories & Slideshows** | **Memories** (*All Memories* or *Favorites*); **Albums** (*Favorites*, *Activity*, or one of the shared albums); **Music Albums** (Apple Music album art); **Style** (transition effects) |
| **Portraits** | people, pets, nature, cities; for People choose all people or Favorites; has an **Update Frequency** ("Change Every"). Apple states: **"Portraits screen savers are only available on Apple TV 4K (2nd generation or later)."** |

Fed by the **default profile's** synced iCloud Photos. tvOS 26 shipped 2025-09-15 and added new India Aerials plus improved iCloud photo-sync fidelity for screen savers.

⚠️ **Trap:** the hardware gate is **not Snoopy-only** — **Portraits** is also gated to Apple TV 4K (2nd gen) or later. That directly constrains any "faces on the big screen" idea built on the system screen saver.

The *"with Preview"* detail on **Style** is **not verbatim in Apple's docs — unverified.**

**Shortcut path:** in the tvOS Photos app you can navigate to **Shared Albums** or **Albums**, select an album, choose **"Set as Screen Saver"**, and confirm — writing straight into the Memories & Slideshows > Albums setting.

⚠️ **HARD CONSTRAINT — there is NO third-party screen-saver API on tvOS.** This is an argument from absence (no Apple statement says "no"), but the absence is consistent across the docs: Top Shelf is the only documented tvOS extension point for this kind of content. **Do not put an Apple TV screen saver on a roadmap.** The screen-saver source is album-shaped, so the *only* system path for our curation is to maintain an actual album (or Shared Album) that the user points the screen saver at.

---

### 18.7 Apple TV — the Photos app on tvOS

Apple's *"Photos app at a glance"* (verbatim): sync iCloud photos to *"view all your photos and videos in full-resolution quality"*; Memories — *"Watch photo memories that highlight collections of photos based on people, places, or moments in time"*; and *"Create a slideshow of your photos with custom transitions and sounds, or use your photos as a screen saver."* Shared Albums (yours and subscribed) are supported.

Setup: first launch prompts to sync all iCloud Photos or only Shared Albums; configured at **Settings > Profiles and Accounts > (default profile) > Photos > iCloud Photos**, requiring confirmation on another Apple device.

⚠️ **Trap (the family-hostile gap):** Apple states outright on that page: **"Only the default profile on Apple TV 4K can sync their iCloud photos."** In a household using tvOS profiles, *everyone else is locked out of Photos entirely.*

⚠️ **Trap:** photos shared from a Mac via **Home Sharing appear in the Computers app, not in Photos.**

The tab names **"Library"** and **"Albums"** are **unverified** — Apple's screen-saver article says to go to *"Shared Albums or Albums at the top of the screen"*, so at minimum a Shared Albums row exists. **"No editing on Apple TV"** is true only by absence; no Apple statement asserts it.

---

### 18.8 Apple TV — the real third-party API surface

**PhotoKit IS available on tvOS.** `PHPhotoLibrary` lists **tvOS 10.0+**. A perfectly ordinary tvOS app can request photo-library authorization and render a full-screen photo/slideshow experience — **no entitlement required, only normal App Store review.**

⚠️ **Trap (corrects a widespread belief, including an earlier draft of this research):** AirPlay is **not** "the only ungated path to the TV." It is only the path that avoids **shipping a tvOS app at all**. The entitlement framing is wrong.

⚠️ **Needs a spike:** no Apple statement was found describing **what a third-party tvOS app actually sees** through PhotoKit (the full synced iCloud library? shared albums only? nothing unless the default profile synced?). Real-world tvOS photo apps (Plex, Google Photos) all source over their own network backends instead. **Verify on hardware before designing around tvOS PhotoKit.**

**Top Shelf** — the one system decoration a tvOS app gets:

- `TVTopShelfContentProvider` (**tvOS 13.0+**) — *"The main interface for your Top Shelf app extension, which you use to provide content for the top shelf area of the tvOS Home Screen."*
- Content types: `TVTopShelfCarouselItem` — *"an item containing images, video, and other information that you want to display using a carousel-based interface"* — and `TVTopShelfSectionedItem`.
- The real API surface for media is the `imageURL` / `previewVideoURL` / `playURL` / `displayURL` properties.

⚠️ **Trap:** two claims in circulation are false. There is **no documented "full-screen Top Shelf variant"** (the documented content types are sectioned and carousel). And the oft-quoted line *"URLs for the pictures or videos you want to display"* **does not appear in Apple's TVServices documentation** — do not quote it.

Top Shelf renders only when **our app icon is focused** on the Home Screen. It is an app-icon decoration, not an ambient system surface, and it is **not** a screen-saver replacement.

---

### 18.9 Vision Pro — spatial scenes, Create Spatial Photo, and the one API Apple gave away

**Spatial scenes (user-facing, visionOS 26+).** Open any photo (2D or spatial), tap the **Spatial Scene button** at the top (Apple also describes it as in the *top-right corner*) of the photo, then tap the **Immersive button** next to it for full immersion; **Exit View** leaves the immersive scene; tapping the Spatial Scene button again removes the effect. Apple: *"Spatial scenes require visionOS 26 or later."* Apple's phrasing for the capability is *"leveraging a new generative AI algorithm and computational depth to create spatial scenes with multiple perspectives, letting users feel like they can lean in and look around."* Spatial scenes also appear in the Spatial Gallery and in **Safari** (spatial browsing turns large images in Reader-capable articles into spatial scenes).

**Create Spatial Photo (persistent conversion, visionOS 2+).** Distinct feature. Verbatim labels: *"Tap the Actions button at the top of the photo, then tap Create Spatial Photo"*; *"Tap Spatial in the bottom-left corner of the photo, then tap Spatial On or Spatial Off"*; to revert, *"Tap the Actions button at the top of the photo, then tap Undo Create Spatial."* ML converts the 2D image into a stereo spatial photo stored as an alternate rendition alongside the original — hence the On/Off toggle and the Undo.

⚠️ **Trap (UX):** these two features are confusingly similar and users mix them up. Do not replicate the split.

**The API — and this is the crown jewel:**

| API | Details |
|---|---|
| `ImagePresentationComponent` | *"A component that supports general image presentation"* — **visionOS 26.0 only** |
| `ImagePresentationComponent.Spatial3DImage` | *"A 3D spatial scene created from a 2D image"* — **visionOS 26.0 only**. Initializers `init(contentsOf:) async throws` (file URL) and `init(imageSource:) async throws` (CGImageSource) |
| `.generate()` | *"Creates a 3D representation of the image if one does not already exist"* — **visionOS 26.0 only** |
| Viewing modes | `desiredViewingMode`: `.mono`, `.spatial3D`, `.spatial3DImmersive`, `.spatialStereo`, `.spatialStereoImmersive` |

RealityKit hands third parties the **same generative 2D→spatial capability Apple ships in its own Photos app**. **No iOS/iPadOS/macOS availability is listed** for any of it.

⚠️ **Trap:** the corpus reports that `generate()` **throws on the visionOS Simulator** and requires real hardware. The fact-checker verified the *availability* facts but did **not** verify the Simulator behaviour — treat "generate() fails in Simulator" as **unverified**, and confirm on a Vision Pro before writing CI expectations around it. Either way, plan for Vision Pro hardware in the test lab.

⚠️ **Trap:** writing a spatial rendition **back into the user's PhotoKit asset** (the way Apple's *Create Spatial Photo* does) is **not exposed**. Third parties get `Spatial3DImage` for **in-app presentation only**. We can, however, write our own spatial/stereo images into the library as *new* assets.

**Photos app structure on visionOS.** A tab bar including **Spatial** (all spatial photos and videos in one place, including spatial photos created from 2D photos) and **Panoramas** (panoramas wrap around you). Spatial media can be shared to another Vision Pro or a compatible iPhone/iPad. Media-type-first navigation, unlike iPhone Photos' collection-first navigation. PhotoKit is available on visionOS 1.0+, so this is fully replicable.

**SharePlay with spatial Personas.** Apple's guide: users can *"use SharePlay in the Photos app with their spatial Persona and enjoy their panoramas, spatial videos, and more — all while feeling like everyone is in the same physical space."* visionOS 26 added shared spatial experiences for **co-located** users in the same room. **GroupActivities is public** and Apple ships an explicit doc, *"Adding spatial Persona support to an activity"* — a third-party visionOS app CAN build spatial-Persona co-viewing.

**Spatial Gallery** (visionOS **2.4**, March 2025). Apple-curated **spatial photos, spatial videos, and panoramas** across **art, culture, entertainment, lifestyle, nature, sports, and travel**; launch partners included Cirque du Soleil, Red Bull, Porsche, and Apple Originals behind-the-scenes.

⚠️ **Trap:** **spatial *scenes* were NOT part of the visionOS 2.4 Spatial Gallery** — spatial scenes only arrived with visionOS 26. And there is **no public submission/publishing API**: the Gallery is editorially curated by Apple. We cannot publish into it.

**WidgetKit gained visionOS 26.0 support** — visionOS widgets are a live third-party place to put an image.

---

### 18.10 The iPhone-adjacent gap: iOS 26 Spatial Scenes has a feature but no API

iOS 26 (shipping; current OS is **iOS 26.5.2**, 26.6 in beta) brings the same generative 2D→3D **Spatial Scenes** effect to the **Lock Screen wallpaper** (parallax as you move the phone). The device floor is **reported as iPhone 12 or later — press-sourced (MacRumors, Engadget), not stated in an Apple doc. Keep the "reported as" hedge and verify before putting it in requirements.**

⚠️ **Trap:** Apple ships the *feature* on iPhone but ships the *API* only on visionOS. There is **no** `ImagePresentationComponent` / `Spatial3DImage` / `generate()` on iOS or macOS. Any third party who wants depth-parallax on iPhone must build their **own monocular depth estimation + parallax rendering**. Apple's iOS feature is also Lock-Screen-wallpaper-only — it is not a way to view your library with depth.

### 18.11 Mac — the organizational features iOS does not have

| Feature | Details | Syncs to iPhone/iPad? |
|---|---|---|
| **Smart Albums** | `File > New Smart Album`. Three pop-up menus per rule: **category / relationship / value** (e.g. category "Photo", "Title", "Date"; operators "is"/"is not"; values like "favorite"). Match **any** or **all** rules. Evaluated continuously — new imports matching the criteria appear automatically. | **NO.** Apple, verbatim: *"Smart Albums that you create on your Mac don't appear in Photos on your iPhone or iPad."* You cannot create a Smart Album on iPhone/iPad at all (true by absence — no such feature is documented in the iPhone/iPad guides). |
| **Folders** | Organize **albums**, not photos. Apple: *"you can create folders to group your albums, and you can also create folders inside other folders."* Shortcut: Option-drag albums onto another album to create a folder. | iPhone/iPad Photos has **no folder creation**. |
| **Multiple libraries** | Hold **Option** at launch to get the Choose Library dialog. | Do not sync. |
| **System Photo Library** | **Photos > Settings > General > "Use as System Photo Library."** Only the System Photo Library syncs via iCloud Photos / Shared Albums / iCloud Shared Photo Library. | — |
| **Referenced mode** | **Photos > Settings > General >** deselect **"Copy items to the Photos library."** Originals stay in place on disk; the library only points at them. **File > Consolidate** copies them in so *"they're easier to back up and are automatically stored in iCloud if iCloud Photos is turned on."* | Referenced files are **NOT uploaded to iCloud Photos** — Apple's library-status article counts them as **"Items on This Mac Only."** |

⚠️ **Trap:** you **cannot move shared albums into a folder.**

⚠️ **Trap (a real footgun):** **switching libraries automatically turns OFF iCloud Photos and Shared Albums.** Any multi-library workflow must warn about this.

⚠️ **Trap (unverified competitive claim):** Apple's Smart Album documentation shows *examples* of criteria but does **not enumerate the full list**, so **whether a Person/Face criterion exists on Mac is UNCONFIRMED.** Do not assert "Apple cannot do person-based smart albums" without checking the app on a physical Mac. The claim we *can* make confidently is the sourced one: **Smart Albums do not sync.**

**Useful:** a Smart Album can filter on **"Photo is referenced"** — the practical way to enumerate referenced-mode originals, directly relevant to a referenced-import feature.

---

### 18.12 Mac — People & Pets management and manual face-box drawing

macOS Photos lets the user **manually add a face the detector missed** — an affordance iOS lacks. All the load-bearing labels below verify against Apple's *"Find and name photos of people and pets on Mac."*

| Action | Exact flow / label |
|---|---|
| Add a missed face | Open the photo → **Info** button → **Add** button → **drag the circle** over the person or pet → click the **Name** field → type a name → press **Return** |
| Resize the circle | Reported as "resize it with the white dot on its side" — ⚠️ **this specific phrasing is unverified** |
| Alternate naming path | **View > Show Face Names** (and **Hide Face Names**), then click *unnamed* under a face and type |
| Reject a wrong identity | **Control-click the circle over the person or pet, then choose "This is Not [name]"** |
| Merge duplicates | **"Merge [number] People"** |
| Confirm more matches | More button → **"Review More Photos"** (Yes / Not confirmation) |
| Other | **"Make Key Photo"**, favorite/hide people, **"Sort by Name"** / **"Sort by Custom Order"**, and featuring a person **less often** |

The circle *is* a face region: the user is literally drawing a face bounding region and attaching an identity, which then propagates to People & Pets. Multiple faces per photo are supported.

⚠️ **Trap:** **PhotoKit does NOT expose face regions or person identities to third parties on any platform.** Apple's face data is reachable only by reading the macOS library database directly.

---

### 18.13 Mac — the `Photos.sqlite` face database (the strategic asset)

The macOS Photos library is a SQLite database: **`Photos.sqlite` on Catalina and later; `Photos.db` on Mojave and older.** The **`ZDETECTEDFACE`** and **`ZPERSON`** tables hold Apple's own face-analysis output. (Photos 4 and earlier used `RKFace` / `RKPerson`.) `osxphotos` (already in our stack) is the maintained abstraction; it joins `ZDETECTEDFACE` ↔ asset table ↔ `ZPERSON` with version-specific handling.

**What `osxphotos`' `FaceInfo` class actually exposes on a modern (Photos 5+) library:**

`uuid`, `name`, `asset_uuid`, `center_x` / `center_y`, `size`, `quality`, `source_width` / `source_height`, `has_smile`, `smile_type`, `manual` (manual-vs-detected flag), `face_type`, `age_type`, `eye_makeup_type`, `eye_state`, `facial_hair_type`, `gender_type`, `glasses_type`, `hair_color_type`, `lip_makeup_type`, `intrash` — plus computed `center`, `size_pixels`, `mwg_rs_area`, `mpri_reg_rect`, and **roll / pitch / yaw**.

⚠️ **Trap — a widely-repeated attribute list is WRONG.** The commonly-cited list conflates the Photos 4 (`RKFace`) schema with the modern one:
- **Eye positions, mouth position, and eye-closure are Photos-4-only.** In `osxphotos`' Photos 5+ path, `ZDETECTEDFACE.ZLEFTEYEX/Y`, `ZRIGHTEYEX/Y`, `ZMOUTHX/Y`, `ZISLEFTEYECLOSED` and `ZISRIGHTEYECLOSED` are **hardcoded to NULL**.
- **There is NO blur score.** `ZBLURSCORE` appears in the SQL but is **not surfaced as a `FaceInfo` attribute**.
- **Scope any face-quality feature to `quality` + roll/pitch/yaw + the type enums.** Do not promise blur/eye/mouth data on a modern library.

⚠️ **Trap:** the schema is **undocumented by Apple and demonstrably changes between macOS releases** (osxphotos already special-cases columns removed in Monterey/Ventura). Pin the osxphotos version and handle schema drift defensively.

⚠️ **Trap:** reading the Photos library requires **Full Disk Access**. And Apple does not populate these tables until its **background analysis has run** — a freshly-imported library may have empty face data.

⚠️ **Trap:** **none of this exists on iOS or Windows.** Do not let it leak into the mobile path.

---

### 18.14 Mac — the write path (extensions, AppleScript) and its blind spot

**Photos extensions — a genuine, supported way for our app to appear *inside* Apple Photos:**

| Extension point | Protocol | Availability |
|---|---|---|
| **Photo editing extension** | `PHContentEditingController` — *"A protocol your custom view controller class implements to provide a user interface for your Photos extension"* (with `PHContentEditingInput`, `PHContentEditingOutput`, `PHAdjustmentData`) | **iOS 8.0+, iPadOS 8.0+, macOS 10.11+, Mac Catalyst 14.0+, visionOS 1.0+. NOT deprecated. NOT available on tvOS.** |
| **Project extension** | `PHProjectExtensionController` — *"A protocol defining the life cycle and supported types of project extensions"* — adds custom "projects" (books, calendars, collages, slideshows) inside Photos | **macOS 10.13+ ONLY. Not deprecated.** |

`PHAdjustmentData` lets a later session reconstruct or revert a prior edit; multiple apps' edits can be layered on one photo. The extension ships inside a host app — installing the app installs the extension.

⚠️ **Trap:** the macOS Photos UI strings for reaching extensions (an **"Extensions"** button in the editing toolbar, **"Manage"**, a **"Photos Editing"** section) are **not verified from Apple documentation — treat as unverified UI vocabulary, not exact labels.**

⚠️ **Trap:** editing extensions are **edit-scoped**. They receive **one asset at a time** and **cannot enumerate the library**. They are a marketing/utility surface, **not a data pipe**.

**AppleScript automation.** macOS Photos exposes an AppleScript dictionary (also usable from JavaScript/Objective-C; wrapped for Python by `RhetTbull/PhotoScript`, actively maintained, latest release v0.5.3, Dec 2025). It can import files, create albums, and manipulate some library structure. PhotoScript's README states verbatim:
- *"it cannot access information on faces in photos"*
- *"nor can it delete a photo"*
- *"Photos does not provide a way to remove a photo from an album"* (PhotoScript fakes removal by recreating the album)

⚠️ **Trap — the asymmetry that defines our Mac integration:** we can **READ** rich face data from `Photos.sqlite` via osxphotos, but we can only **WRITE** through AppleScript/PhotoKit — and **AppleScript explicitly cannot touch faces and cannot delete**, while **PhotoKit does not expose person/face writing either**. Therefore: **face/identity corrections are a strictly ONE-WAY import from Apple Photos into our app. We can enrich; we cannot repair Apple's People album.** Set product expectations accordingly.

---

### 18.15 Windows — iCloud for Windows (the largest greenfield in the domain)

Apple ships **iCloud for Windows** via the **Microsoft Store**. With Photos enabled, iCloud photos surface **inside the Microsoft Photos app** (sidebar item **"iCloud Photos"**). Shared Albums are supported: create a new shared album, invite subscribers, manage subscribers, and — verbatim Apple option — **"Create a public website to allow anyone to view these photos on iCloud.com."**

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Microsoft Store app system requirement | **Windows 10 version 1903 / build 18362.145 or later, or Windows 11; 64-bit.** ⚠️ **Trap:** the often-quoted **"Windows 10 build 14393"** is the *older/general* iCloud-for-Windows floor and is **misleading for the Store app.** |
| Files land at `C:\Users\<user>\Pictures\iCloud Photos\Photos` | Sourced |
| OneDrive-displaced variant path `C:\Users\<user>\iCloud Photos\Photos` | **UNVERIFIED** against Apple's current guide |
| Shared Albums sync to a `\Shared` subfolder | **UNVERIFIED** against Apple's current guide |
| The **"Show iCloud Photos"** toggle (Microsoft Photos app Settings > Personalization) | **UNVERIFIED** — third-party-documented only |
| iCloud Shared Photo Library supported on Windows | **UNVERIFIED** — no Apple statement found either way |

**The important fact:** iCloud for Windows is a **file-sync client plus a shell/Photos-app integration**. It is **not** the Photos app. There is **no on-device analysis**: **no People/faces, no Memories, no ML/semantic search, no Portrait/depth features, no editing parity.** On Windows there is **literally no competitor feature to beat — only an absence to fill.**

⚠️ **Trap:** on Windows there is **no `ZPERSON` database to bootstrap from.** Windows users get **zero pre-labeled people**. Cold-start onboarding must not assume Apple's labels exist.

---

### 18.16 Web (iCloud.com), CarPlay, Android, and the unshipped smart display

**Photos on iCloud.com** — confirmed capabilities from Apple's iCloud user guide: browse **Library**, albums and folders from the sidebar; **Memories** (select *Memories* in the sidebar → *See All*, with a **Favorite Memories** filter; play/pause/restart); switch between personal library, shared library, or both (iCloud Shared Photo Library); **"Add or edit a title, caption, or other metadata"**; create albums and folders; favorite; upload and download; create and manage shared albums and **iCloud Links**; like and comment on shared album photos; **"Play a slideshow of photos"**; change video playback quality; delete and recover.

⚠️ Apple's guide documents **no People/faces browser and no photo editing** on the web. (Argument from absence — but the absence is real and consistent across the guide.)

⚠️ **Trap / architectural bedrock:** **there is NO public iCloud Photos API for third parties.** Apple provides no way for a third party to read a user's iCloud photo library from a server or from Windows. The only paths that exist are **on-device PhotoKit** and **the local macOS library**. Anyone proposing "just talk to iCloud from the server" should be shown this sentence.

**CarPlay — a permanent dead end.** Framework abstract, verbatim: *"Integrate CarPlay in apps related to audio, communication, navigation, parking, EV charging, food ordering, and more."* Documented entitlement-gated categories: **audio, communication, navigation, parking, EV charging, food ordering** (plus driving-task / fueling / roadside categories in the CarPlay app programming guide). CarPlay is template-driven and entitlement-gated; apps must be explicitly approved for a category. **There is no photo, gallery, or image-viewing template or entitlement — and displaying a photo gallery to a driver is a road-safety non-starter.** Remove it from the backlog permanently.

**Android** — Apple ships **no Photos surface on Android at all**, beyond iCloud.com in a browser. (Android 17 shipped stable 2026-06-16.)

**HomePod / the reported Apple smart display — DO NOT PLAN FOR IT.** HomePod and HomePod mini have no display, therefore no photo surface. The reported Apple smart-home hub (≈7-inch square display, wall-mountable or on a HomePod-mini-style base, with a camera, running a new OS, described in reporting as able to display photos) **has NOT shipped as of 2026-07-14 and Apple has announced no such product.** The most recent reporting (Bloomberg/Gurman, 9 March 2026) says it was **pushed from a planned March 2026 introduction to around September 2026** because the revamped Siri isn't ready. ⚠️ **This is entirely press reporting on unreleased hardware — zero Apple documentation, no OS, no SDK, no announced third-party app model. It must appear on no roadmap and in no deck.**

### 18.17 Cross-surface capability matrix

| Surface | Can a 3rd party read the photo library? | Ambient/system surface available to us? | Apple's own photo intelligence present? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **watchOS** | **No** — `PHPhotoLibrary` unavailable. `PhotosPicker` (watchOS 9.0+) only. Real pipe = `WCSession.transferFile` | Complications / Smart Stack widgets via WidgetKit (⚠️ `accented` rendering). **No watch-face API**; `CLKWatchFaceLibrary` imports only pre-authored, bundle-embedded `.watchface` files | Album-scoped sync only; no search, no People on the watch |
| **tvOS** | **Yes, nominally** — `PHPhotoLibrary` tvOS 10.0+ (⚠️ what it actually sees is **unverified; needs a hardware spike**) | **Top Shelf only** (`TVTopShelfContentProvider`, tvOS 13.0+). **No screen-saver API** | Memories + screen saver, **default-profile-only**, no search, no People tab, no editing |
| **visionOS** | **Yes** — PhotoKit visionOS 1.0+ | WidgetKit (visionOS 26.0+); GroupActivities spatial Personas. Cannot publish into Spatial Gallery | Spatial scenes (visionOS 26+), Create Spatial Photo (visionOS 2+) — **and `Spatial3DImage.generate()` is handed to third parties** |
| **macOS** | **Yes, richly** — PhotoKit + **direct `Photos.sqlite` read** (faces!) via osxphotos (needs Full Disk Access) | Photo editing extension (`PHContentEditingController`) + **project extension** (`PHProjectExtensionController`, Mac-only) | Full: People & Pets with manual face boxes, Smart Albums, folders, referenced libraries |
| **Windows** | N/A — files on disk | N/A | **NONE.** File sync only |
| **iCloud.com** | **No public API** | N/A | Memories + search; **no People browser, no editing** documented |
| **CarPlay** | **No — and never will be** | None | None |
| **Android** | N/A | None | **None** (browser only) |
